speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should like to express my thanks to the committee for permission to continue. I will try to make my remarks very brief.
In this regard, I should like to refer very briefly to the remarks of the hon. member for Peterborough. I do not wish to be accused of taking the hon. member's remarks out of context, and I shall most certainly attempt not to do that. However, there are one or two observations made by the hon. member which are pertinent. On page 8090 of Hansard for September 7 of this year I find the following statement:
However, we have no right to expect that West Berlin can be continued as a means of subverting the East German government. If it becomes a matter of helping to oppress people by our foreign policy we are going to be in serious difficulties indeed, as this will mean real war.
Regardless of the interpretation one might put on that particular observation, I think it is safe to say that it would seem clear, in my mind at least, that the hon. member for Peterborough feels the western nations are in some way trying to oppress the poor people of East Germany who, of course, have no means of defending themselves. This may be a wrong interpretation, but I feel it is the one that must be put on these remarks. Later on the same page the hon. member is reported to have said:
Mr. Khrushchev is not Hitler. He does not have the power.
I do not know about that. Perhaps the hon. member's source of information is different from mine, but it would certainly seem to me that Mr. Khrushchev has a considerable
Supply-External Affairs amount of power. Then on page 8091 the hon. member is reported to have said, referring to NATO:
We agree with that and we agree that it has played a real part.
He used the past tense. Perhaps nothing was meant by putting this in the past tense, but I feel no other interpretation can be put on those remarks but that NATO has been valuable in the past and will not be of much value in the future. A little later on the same page the hon. member is reported as saying:
On the other hand when we see the resumption of nuclear tests-
He is referring to NATO.
-we cannot see this as defensive at all-
I find difficulty in following that reasoning in view of the fact that it was the Soviet union, as everyone knows, that resumed the testing. I think everyone would agree that it would be the rankest folly if the United States authorities felt tests of a certain nature, underground ones, should not be carried out if the Soviet union were gaining a military advantage by its renewed tests. These remarks by themselves perhaps are not too important, but I think they do reflect a state of mind which must exist among a number of members of the new party. The hon. member has specifically designated himself as a new party man and not a member of the C.C.F. I believe, therefore, the public is really entitled to further clarification of the actual stand of that party. Certainly the impression one would gather is that, to say the least, there is only lukewarm support for NATO's past performance, and if the chips were down there might not be very much support at all.
Remarks were made by some other hon. members referring to Canada in two ways. One reference was to Canada's role as the linchpin between the Soviet union and the United States. Another was that Canada should be the waiter at the door holding the door open for the two to go back and forth between each other's dining rooms. While I do not for a moment question the sincerity of these suggestions, I think there is a certain misconception. The misconception is that Canada is a neutral country, and I should hope not in the connotation "neutral" has acquired lately. We are a member of NATO. Under the present circumstances I do not really know how anybody could expect the Soviet union, for instance, to accept Canada as a linchpin or neutral country in some sort of negotiation between the United States and the Soviet union. Canada is not a neutral country. I do not think Russia would be prepared to accept us in that role, any more than we would be prepared to accept Rumania in the same
8164	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs role. This misconception that Canada is neutral is something that I think goes back to past history.
As I understand it, at the time the Leader of the Opposition was making his very famous and excellent contribution to the United Nations, Canada and Norway were among the countries which played a very active part in negotiations at that organization. At that time the membership of the United Nations was relatively small; it was about half the size it is now, and was very heavily dominated by western nations. Countries like Canada and Norway had the reputation of making good, sound, sensible suggestions. At that time the Soviet union was undoubtedly prepared to have Canada make certain suggestions.
However, the picture is quite different now. There are all these new, independent countries in the world, and a great many of them have varying degrees of neutralist views ranging to the extreme. These are the countries to which the Soviet union now looks, I think, rather than to ourselves; because clearly we are a part of NATO and it is very difficult for us to retain this role any longer in view of changed world conditions.
I do not think there is very much point in any of us living in a fool's paradise and thinking we have this position when in fact we probably no longer have it. I am not suggesting that Canada's good offices and Canada's suggestions are not acceptable at the United Nations. They are; very much so. At the United Nations our advice is constantly sought on many things. However, I do not think we still have the public role that perhaps we had a number of years ago, for the reasons I have suggested.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Niagara Falls, when making her speech the other night, made reference to the Scotch song, "I Know Where I'm Going". The hon. member suggested that perhaps we do not know where we are going. I may agree with that to a certain extent. But certainly the Soviet union knows where it is going. Ever since 1919 the ultimate objectives of the Soviet union have been abundantly clear. They are communisation of the world. There has never been any denying that. It is quite true that the paths to attain that objective change as circumstances change from day to day and year to year, but the ultimate objective is the same.
I remember one little conversation I overheard in New York between two delegates, who of course shall be nameless. One delegate was teasing a delegate of the Soviet group countries. He said, "I hear you are having a little trouble with China lately". This was last fall. The other delegate said, "Yes, that


is quite true; we are having a little argument with China. But I do not know what you are happy about, because after all the only argument is the best way to liquidate you people". I think frankness such as that is at least something that can be appreciated.
Dictatorships always have the advantage of being on the offensive. Democracies always have to move more slowly. We are on the defensive. The Soviet union has a planned objective and everything is directed toward that objective. They do startling and dynamic things. Certainly the leader of the Soviet union at the present time has all the showmanship abilities of the late P. T. Barnum; there are no two ways about that. Also, the speed with which the Soviet union acts and what it does are impressive and appeal to a great many neutralist countries.
It is no use fooling ourselves about this. The Soviet union, because of its achievements and quick action, gets a certain amount of fear, but it also gets respect and a certain amount of admiration from these neutralist countries. It has always been the same through history when there has been a society that is aggressive and dynamic. That has appealed to some people.
As the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo pointed out a few minutes ago, this is something we have to make clear to this country and to all the western world. It is no use just saying, "The Soviet union is wrong and we are right". These neutralist countries are not buying it. The Prime Minister has repeatedly pointed out on different occasions that the west must get a positive plan to sell to the rest of the world. As yet this has not been taken up. I hope that Canada, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, will continue to press for this and that the west will come up with a dynamic policy that will be bought by these other countries. It is no use just being on the defensive all the time, because if we are, I am afraid the ultimate results are clear.
Let me again refer to the question of Berlin. One hon. member said, "It is no use going to war over Berlin". That is quite true; it is not, over Berlin. I remember, as I am sure other hon. members of the house remember, the years 1936, 1937 and 1938. We saw Hitler coming along. First it was the Rhineland, then Austria, Czechoslovakia and Poland. It was not over Poland as such that Britain and France went to war with Germany. It was because the line which could not be crossed had to be drawn. I remember at that time we said "We have learned our lesson this time. We will never let it happen again." Ever since world war II we have seen nothing but this same attitude,

the peculiar idea that we can appease dictatorships. Instead of appeasement, however, all we do is whet their appetites.
We have seen this all through history since the dark ages. It happened in Great Britain when the Danes were attacking the coast of Britain. It was thought that the Danes could be bought off with gold. Well, the Danes took the gold and came back the next year for more. We are facing the same kind of situation now. In the experience I have had dealing with representatives of the Soviet union I have found they are tough and very practical people who will try anything if they think it will succeed. I thoroughly agree with the view expressed by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that in the present situation we must be tough, but calm and resolute, and we must not panic. This is something the Soviet union understands and respects. If we keep our powder dry and remain firm in our stand I think negotiations can succeed and will succeed.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to participate in this debate at the present time. However, the remarks which have just ended have made me rise. In the first place I wish to express my personal good wishes to our Secretary of State of External Affairs. I believe all Canada realizes the heavy burdens that are resting upon him. When he leads our delegation at the United Nations next week and for the weeks thereafter I believe all Canadians will wish him every success in his endeavours. I hope the men and women associated with him on behalf of our nation will exert their greatest efforts to reflect the attitude and policies that our minister has put forward on so many occasions in the past.
I very much regret that I noticed a considerable divergence of view between the speech just concluded by the parliamentary secretary and the attitude and views that have hitherto been expressed by the minister himself. I hope this is going to be looked into. I know the minister has appointed a new man to replace the hon. member as the deputy leader at the United Nations. I hope the man now appointed to be the deputy leader of the Canadian delegation will very honestly, sincerely and fairly represent the attitude of the minister in the dealings he will necessarily have from day to day with the representatives of other nations.
I believe in essence the hon. member for Oxford attempted to paint the world situation as a contest between capitalism and communism. I am glad this is not the basic conflict in the world of today, even though people in Moscow and in Washington would like to make it such. The vast majority of the world's
Supply-External Affairs population of today believe not only in political democracy, but also in economic and social democracy. These people outnumber the people in the communist bloc and in the bloc that is dominated by the United States of America. I predict that eventually these people who are interested in economic and social democracy in addition to political democracy are going to win the day. I hope they can win the day without the holocaust of nuclear war that either the communist or the capitalist world may attempt to launch in the world.
I think the hon. member for Oxford ought to do a bit of homework. He spoke at length on the external affairs policy of the new party. I assume he meant the New Democratic party. As his source of information he used an interpretation placed on our external affairs policy by the Montreal Gazette. May I inform him that the New Democratic party does not own the Montreal Gazette. It is more likely than not that the hon. member's own Tory party owns the Montreal Gazette. May I say that this is a very poor source of information as to what our foreign policy is.
The hon. member attempted to brand us as neutralists. We are not neutralists by any stretch of the imagination. In the world of today democracy could not survive without the ardent support the social democrats the world over are giving to the cause of political democracy. However, because we wish to extend political democracy, the capitalists of the world love to smear us and brand us as neutralists, pro-communists and all the other names they can invent.
The hon. member spoke of our policy on NATO. I will admit that our movement has reservations about NATO. If NATO is going to be nothing more than a mere tool in the hands of the Pentagon; if NATO is going to desert those in western Europe who believe in democracy then the earlier we get out of NATO, the better. Many of the delegates at the United Nations have repeatedly expressed to me their disappointment at what is happening to the NATO organization. The people who believe in democracy in Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Germany and France have severe reservations as to the course that is being pursued by NATO. Canada could help its allies in western Europe if, to use the term used by the hon. member, the Canadian government had the guts to stand for what the Canadian people believe in instead of echoing, time after time, the intentions and the aspirations of those who rule the roost in the Pentagon.
NATO has played a most useful role in our history. However, may I remind the government that acts of aggression have been committed within the past five or six years by

Supply-External Affairs member nations of the western world in greater number than those that have been committed by members of the communist bloc.
I am unwilling to forgive the communist bloc for those acts of aggression. I know they have occurred, and they are unforgivable. But those that the capitalist world have committed are equally unforgivable. Today across the line in their magazines it is openly admitted that the United States government intervened in the affairs of the Cuban people. At the time the event occurred we were expected to believe that our ally and, as I still say, our good neighbour to the south had nothing to do with the attempt to overthrow the government in that other nation. However, today their magazines gloat over their effort, and are beginning to analyse the reasons for their failure.
We will continue to support NATO if NATO is going to abide by its original intent, namely to act as a brake against potential communist expansion in western Europe, as was originally intended, and not as an instrument to launch a nuclear war. If it is going to act as a brake against potential communist expansion in western Europe, and if it is going to help to establish a little more economic unity in the western world, we will continue to support it. But let us make no mistake about the matter. The moment that NATO begins to adopt nuclear weapons-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

-our movement and, I am sure, the Canadian people with us will oppose NATO. NATO was never intended to be an organization that might be responsible for blowing the whole world to bits. We say that no Canadian should be equipped with nuclear weapons either here or abroad. We say that nuclear weapons should never be permitted either on or above Canadian territory.
I should like to ask the government this question. How much truth is there in the newspaper reports I read yesterday to the effect that United States planes loaded with nuclear weapons are flying regular operations above Canadian territory? We at one time had an assurance from this government that for each and every such single flight a specific permit was required and was granted by the government of Canada. Does that situation hold good today? The Canadian people would like to have an answer. We had only a few days ago a report or a listing of the number of occasions on which nuclear weapons were accidentally almost exploded.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There was no accident about the explosion of nuclear weapons in Russia in the last few days.

We recognize the fact that the Russians have them, that the Americans have them and that the French have them. However, what we say is this. Let not any more of us have them. We have enough of them in existence in the world. What possible useful contribution could Canada make by adding to the existing amount of nuclear weapons the world has today? Already there are in the hands of the great nations of the world from 10 to 20 tons of t.n.t. for every man, woman and child in the world. Hence what useful contribution can we make, except an attempt to be big shots on the world scene? The Canadian people do not appreciate this sense of haste. As the Prime Minister has said, this is a time for brakemanship. These sabre rattling speeches in this House of Commons serve no useful purpose whatsoever. Washington and Moscow do not even listen to them, because they do not have to listen.
We ought to take a different attitude and approach. We ought to express our regrets and make it clear that we will defend the political democracy, which was won for us by our forefathers at such heavy cost, with our lives if necessary. However, to go beyond that position with appeals to military power on our part; appeals to individuals who believe they can survive a nuclear war; appeals to armament manufacturers, and appeals to a limited number of Canadian people, makes no useful contribution to the cause of world peace.
In respect to Berlin-and I am pleased that the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo identified his attitude in this regard as being his own and not the official attitude of the Liberal party-that hon. member suggested we must work toward the reunification of Berlin. I believe I know something about the philosophy of the German race, and I will make this prediction. With a reunified Germany today we will have a Germany tomorrow seeking not only revenge but the re-establishment of the old glory of the German reich, as it was once known, and the world will once again be thrown into a war.
I certainly agree that the people of Germany ought to be reunited if this can be done by peaceful means. However, I suggest the situation in Berlin is not now a threat to world peace of the magnitude painted by the United States press. No leading statesman has yet claimed an intention of bringing West Berlin under communist domination. No leading statesman has claimed that access by the West Berliners to East Berlin and East Berliners to West Berlin ought to be blocked. On the contrary, there has been an offer to guarantee access.

I suggest we should supply the initiative in this regard. We should state that past history has shown us we have reason to doubt the word of communism, and that pledges have not always been kept. We should state that we are unable to afford the further risk of a broken promise regarding the availability of access, and it must therefore be made to the United Nations, allowing that organization to ensure continued liberty in West Berlin so that in the event the communist state breaks its word it will then have offended not only the west but this world organization, with the result that the whole world will know the reliability of promises made by a communist regime.
The real issue in Berlin is the reunification of Germany, and the Canadian people state that the reunification of Germany is not worth fighting a world war for, with all its consequences. The people of Canada are unwilling to go to war for the attainment of a reunified Germany. They are willing to go to war if necessary to defend political democracy, but that is not the issue involved. The issue involves a close alliance between Washington and Bonn, and the Canadian people realize this in their hearts. That is the basic issue, and Canadian people ought to be informed of it.
If the west desires to make a useful contribution to world peace let it be stated to Russia that it will pull out of West Germany if Russia will do likewise in respect to East Germany, allowing the German people to settle their own problems. The borders could be guarded by the United Nations. Let it be further stated that such a reunified Germany should be forever without armaments. This was done in respect to Austria, and I suggest it can be done in the case of Germany.
I suggest the western world made the worst possible mistake when it agreed to rearm West Germany. When that was done it caused the postponement for possibly many years of any possibility of the reunification of Eastern and Western Germany, because in all logic the communists cannot be expected to withdraw their forces from East Germany as long as the forces of the west are stationed in West Germany and, even worse, as long as West Germany is growing in military might with an increasing attitude of aggressiveness as far as international forces are concerned.
I suggest our position is very clear. We are prepared to defend political democracy, but are not and never have been prepared to defend the interests of the international cartels; the oil monopolies, the chemical monopolies and those other monopolies with head offices in the United States of America.
Supply-External Affairs We believe with the peoples of Israel, the Scandinavian countries and social democratic forces of the world over, that we can only build world peace if war is avoided, because if war comes no one will build anything.
I was very much heartened by the words of a spokesman of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona who is reported at page 8136 of Hansard of September 8, 1961 as follows:
Therefore peaceful coexistence is the only existence there is. It is not an alternate form of action; it is the only possibility.
Hon. members in this group say hear, hear to that statement. It will not be the world of the west or of the east, but a new world in the event of a nuclear war, and that hon. member's statement epitomizes the basic policy of our hope.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, the events of the last few weeks have added a seriousness to the manner in which debates are conducted in this house. This was apparent in the contribution made by all hon. members who have voiced their views as to the ways to peace. In particular I want to refer to the Leader of the Opposition, who along with the hon. member from Essex East placed before the committee his views on this very important matter in a way that was in keeping with the responsibilities that rest on all of us, including the government of the day.
I am going to resist the invitation given by the last hon. gentleman to enter at this time into controversial things, since there will be an opportunity later on to deal with some of the matters to which he referred and also some of the references by other hon. gentlemen of the New Democratic party, who as a result of the changes that took place at a recent convention find themselves in a position difficult to explain; for the policies of March, April and May on NATO, as enunciated by the responsible leader of the former C.C.F. party, have gone through a metamorphosis that makes it somewhat difficult for those hon. gentlemen to square their consciences of May, June and July with the practical results of the changes that took place during that historic meeting. All I can say is that had we followed the advice given by the leader of the C.C.F. in those months in regard to NATO, in the light of the changes that have taken place I can see now how wrong we would have been. However, it is not of

Supply-External Affairs that that I intend to speak today. I am going to discuss in general something of the situation that faces us and something of the problems that we as members of parliament must meet.
I repeat what I said a moment ago. The thanks of the committee are due to all hon. members for the way in which they dealt with this very important question not only of West Berlin but of the world situation generally and the several things referred to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in outlining matters for the consideration of the committee. I am not going into the field of defence today, or of measures that are being taken for national survival. These will be dealt with when the departmental estimates in which these matters are dealt with come before the committee. I want to say further in that connection that I appreciate the co-operation of the opposition and the attitude taken by all members of the opposition in permitting the motion for supply to go through this morning without debate in order to ensure that there would be no delay in the discussion of those questions of national and international importance that face us today.
I thank the Leader of the Opposition for the contribution he made in answering some myths that have achieved widespread circulation during recent weeks. One of them is that Berlin is a crisis that propaganda built, a view expressed by one or more journalists or pundits in various parts of Canada. The other is that Canadians are the victims of propaganda to make them believe there is a crisis over Berlin. The Leader of the Opposition dealt effectively with those who hold that view. In his attitude and in that of the hon. member for Essex East they gave an indication of the seriousness with which they view the international situation, and the need of each and every one of us to make the best contribution possible without regard to political considerations.
The Leader of the Opposition made some reference to a speech I made recently before the Canadian Bar Association, and gave general approval thereto. I can only say that this is one time I most heartily reciprocate the words he used, when he stated that he thought I struck the right note. In order to keep in harmony with that attitude, I say of him as he said of me that in his speech in the house the other day I thought he struck the right note.
While differences are bound to occur between government and opposition, differences which are a vital necessity of democratic government, there does come a time when issues transcend political considerations, and this is one of those times. All of us have as our purpose and our aim the maintenance and

the preservation of peace. Those of us who have responsibilities would like to do that which we are often asked to do, go into detail in regard to matters, when if we did that the result would be to deny that freedom of consultation which is of the essence of the relationship that must prevail among the free nations.
My opinion, and I think the attitude of the house, has been that this is an hour which demands moral strength and courage. Panic is the refuge of weakness. Confidence can be a weapon of peace. Communism breeds on fear and weakness. When I hear criticism of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization I sometimes wonder whether those who criticize realize that if it had not been for the defensive strength of NATO we might very well not be here today. That is how important NATO has been as a defensive organization, and how necessary it is today.
The ideals of democracy and peace in my opinion can best be served at this hour by showing the Kremlin that we will not sit back and allow the world in which we believe to be swept aside by the acceptance of those things that deny every principle of freedom for which we stand. We must at the same time speak words of measured carefulness so that nothing will be said which will add to the fires which today are burning.
Mr. Chairman, in the past two days the house has maintained that principle, that each and all of us have to speak and must speak our views. That is the essence of democracy. Some of us will have to go back on some of the views that we have expressed in the past. That is of the essence of democracy too. Though I do not often do so, I speak now of a colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and of the contribution he has made since assuming that office, a contribution outstanding and worthy of the sacrifice made by those of his generation who served with him in the first war. He believed in the United Nations, and in the United Nations and outside he built a structure of peace with disarmament. He carried the fight in the United Nations and at Geneva. That is why his speech the other day to me carried the conviction that comes from one who is speaking with the experience that he has had.
I see that some say he retreated. There is no retreat when one acknowledges that the idealism that he has expressed has not been accepted, and has been interpreted by the Kremlin and those associated with the Kremlin as a sign of weakness rather than of greatness. Some say he is too idealistic. Idealism has its place, Mr. Chairman, and if the free world sacrifices its idealism to godless materialism there will be little to

choose between communism and democracy in 50 years, whatever the result may be of the world contest. With all his heart, with all his devotion to the principle of disarmament, and with all his hopefulness that the clouds on the international horizon would be dissipated, in the light of recognition of the terrible danger of a nuclear war he told the house that we in the free world were on the threshold of potential world disaster.
That causes us to re-examine some of the principles of Canada's foreign policy which, in the light of the discussions that have taken place during this debate, indicate an area of agreement between the government and the opposition, with the opposition having at all times not only the right but the duty to point out, while agreeing with the objectives, what changes should be made that would be beneficial.
Canada's foreign policy can be summed up in three short paragraphs: First, continuing support for a strong and effective United Nations without which peace cannot be achieved, while recognizing that changes in the charter such as were indicated by the hon. member for Oxford ought to be made in the light of the experience since 1945. Second, the need of a strong and effective North Atlantic Treaty Organization, with which I will deal later. Finally, and I speak now for the government in this regard, we believe in the extension and development of a strong commonwealth of nations, believing that no other association throughout the world has a greater influence for good. Indeed, the adherence by its members to its principles, though unwritten, denies the acceptance of communism.
The position we are in today, and when I say this I speak of the attitude of some Canadians and others, is brought about as a result of the process of confusion and propaganda which is of the essence of communist philosophy. The communists deceive people into believing that the existing crisis was created by other nations.
There is no disagreement between the government and the opposition, Mr. Chairman, that the crisis was created by Khrushchev for his own purposes, just as he has created crises throughout the years. If it is not Korea it is Vie Nam. If it is not Vie Nam it is Berlin, and so on. There is no crisis of our making in East Berlin. We have not stirred up any crisis. Some say to me: "How can Canada consider doing anything else but bending the knee to Khrushchev over a paltry city of 2.5 million?" I quite understand the sentimental and emotional plea behind that. The sacrifice of 100,000 Canadians cannot but bring that emotional reaction if the broader situation is not examined.
Supply-External Affairs
This is a larger question than West Berlin, a greater problem than its people. There is the pledged word of the western nations that the people of West Berlin will not be sacrificed, their freedom will not be destroyed; that the rights of access into West Berlin shall not be discontinued. Berlin has become the tangible symbol of a global difference between communism and the forces of freedom. The U.S.S.R. would endeavour to restrict the problem to a divided Berlin. Berlin is more than an isolated outpost. Khrushchev knows that he has already sealed off ingress and egress to West Berlin from East Berlin. He has done that because he realized that the outcome in connection with Berlin will determine, in a considerable measure, the future of freedom everywhere in the world.
When one walks in the streets of West Berlin it is difficult to realize that to thinking people everywhere in the world this small island, as it were, surrounded by communism, represents to the free world, as it represents to the communist world, the axis of the struggle as between communism and freedom. It is not a question of the reunification of Germany, as was mentioned here this morning. We are not dealing with that question. We are dealing with the pledged word of the free world. If we ever get the reputation amongst the uncommitted nations of the world that are standing with us that our word, under seal, means no more than a passing fancy, then indeed will Khrushchev have won the greatest victory communism has ever achieved.
One has to follow the course he has taken since the adjournment of the house, and it has been an interesting course. From time to time he has spoken the soft, sweet words of peace. These were followed by threats as to what would happen. One moment he is the smiling Khrushchev; the next moment he is engaged in his terror campaign. It is difficult to understand why he chose a time just before the Belgrade conference opened to announce the resumption of his nuclear testing program. Perhaps his purpose was to make the neutrals fearful that if they were critical of the U.S.S.R. they would be in danger. Why did he take that course? Well, he must have been preparing for some time because we were told today, I believe, that the fifth and sixth atomic explosions had occurred. Is he about to announce the production of an anti-missile missile following a short period of testing?
It is interesting to note that some of those who speak the loudest regarding the stand of Canada and the free world have been so silent in their condemnation of Khrushchev and the stand he has taken followed by his action regarding nuclear testing. He has

Supply-External Affairs placed the lives of people everywhere in the world in jeopardy. He has done so cynically. He said his purpose was, in effect, to let the people of the world realize their position and their danger. I find it difficult to understand, as did the Secretary of State for External Affairs, why the Belgrade conference did not make some outstanding declarations on this subject. I find it difficult to understand how they reacted so tepidly to Khrushchev's gross contempt of human safety.
The United States is now proceeding with testing. I have my own views in this regard. I can only say one thing. I hope that no action will be taken by any government belonging to the NATO organization without consultation in advance of that action. I realize that, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has pointed out, they could take no other course. It is not for me to say that one would have hoped that having delayed for three years during the moratorium, a delay of the same number of weeks might have been helpful in the mobilization of world opinion.
What is Khrushchev's attitude? I am often told that if we could only try and be reasonable, how different things would be. Was there anything unreasonable in the request made by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and the President of the United States that there be no testing in the atmosphere? Testing in the atmosphere, the cause of the deleterious nature of fall-out, should have been the last thing undertaken. There could have been tests underground. Mr. Khrushchev declared on Saturday that nuclear testing could be ended only by western acceptance of Soviet proposals for a German peace treaty and complete disarmament. What association is there between nuclear testing and a German peace treaty?
For the last year and a half the Secretary of State for External Affairs has been doing everything possible, as I said a moment ago, to bring about international agreement on disarmament. The Leader of the Opposition pointed out there were 300 or so meetings held in Geneva. There was hope. I remember the last time I talked to Prime Minister Macmillan. He said, "I think we are going to secure a continuing moratorium and indeed an agreement on testing." If we had been able to achieve that, we would have gone a long way, because we would have established that in this narrow field, inspection and control would operate in an experimental stage as a preparation for the larger field of disarmament whenever disarmament comes.
Mr. Khrushchev called on the United States and Great Britain to meet in settling the main problems of our times, general and complete disarmament. He said, "Let us seek
[Mr, Diefenbaker.J
seriously, in good faith, a solution of the question of concluding a German peace treaty so as to arrest in good time the sliding of states into the inferno of a rocket nuclear war". In other words, "I believe in negotiation", says Mr. Khrushchev. He says, "I will keep what I have and then I will take what you have or part of it". That is not the principle of negotiation.
What has his attitude been since last July, when the house last met? He has been moving to higher and more aggressive peaks of threat and intimidation week by week. It is very interesting to read the communist manifesto. I am not going into details with regard thereto, but I suggest to hon. members that they read the text of the Soviet party's draft program for the next 20 years. Hitler took 1,000 pages in "Mein Kampf". Khrushchev takes less than 50 pages, and he places before the world the blueprint of the architect, in which be builds a house for all mankind, with the U.S.S.R. having the only key to the premises.
It is well to read what he says. It reveals the cold ruthlessness that is apparent in the breaking of his nation's word by the resumption of tests. Today one hon. member said this is not a contest between capitalism and socialism. I immediately rise to say that in so far as communism is concerned it would bring about all its changes by revolution, infiltration and the destruction of the will to resist. This is what the Soviet party's draft program says:
The great October socialist revolution ushered in a new era in the history of mankind, the era of the downfall of capitalism and the establishment of communism. Socialism has triumphed in the Soviet union and has achieved decisive victories in the people's democracies; socialism has become a cause of practical significance to hundreds of millions of people, and the bearer of the revolutionary movement of the working class throughout the world.
Then it goes on to say:
The socialist revolution in European and Asian countries has resulted in the establishment of the world socialist system. A powerful wave of national liberation revolutions is sweeping away the colonial system of imperialism.
One does not have to sort out these
passages:
The victorious workers and peasants lacked knowledge of state administration and the experience necessary for the construction of a new society. The difficulties of socialist construction were greatly increased by the fact that for almost 30 years the U.S.S.R. was the world's only socialist state, and was subjected to incisive attacks by the hostile capitalist environment.
Then it says again:
Socialism has done away forever with the supremacy of private ownership of the means of production, that source of the division of society into antagonistic classes. Socialist ownership of the means of production has become the solid

economic foundation of society. Unlimited opportunities have been afforded for the development of the productive forces.
Then it also says:
Under the leadership of Lenin it worked out a plan for the radical transformation of the country, for the construction of socialism. On the basis of a thorough scientific analysis, Lenin elaborated the policy of the proletarian state for the entire period of transition from capitalism to socialism. He evolved the new economic policy (N.E.P.), designed to bring about the victory of socialism.
And so Khrushchev goes on. He says that within this generation the Kremlin will have succeeded everywhere in the world in bringing about the changes that are set out in that manifesto. He also indicates that coexistence means the acceptance by the free world of the will of the communist world.
1 think all of us are agreed as to the seriousness of the events of recent days. What should be done? There have been a number of suggestions made, all of them helpful. I am not going into a detailed analysis in any way of the matters that were referred to by the hon. members who spoke, and in particular those questions that were propounded by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East. I am, however, going to say something regarding the possibility of the United Nations having a larger place in an endeavour to bring about a settlement of this problem.
There are some things the United Nations can do; there are others it cannot do. The United Nations is limited by the fact that Berlin is part of the peace settlement with Germany and is therefore, under the charter, reserved for consideration by the victorious powers. However, if the four powers decide they would like the United Nations to play a part, then there are roles the United Nations can play. There is the question of safeguarding the maintenance of peace; and where the peace is threatened, if the mapor-ity of the United Nations decide that this is being done by the U.S.S.R. or by any other nation, the matter could be brought before the United Nations. Mr. Khrushchev said in his interview with Mr. Sulzberger of the New York Times that he is not averse to United Nations discussions if the big four agree.
Various suggestions have been made. One is that the whole of the city of Berlin could be placed under the trusteeship of the United Nations, with access guaranteed by a U.N. force. There have been suggestions that the United Nations should be moved from New York to Berlin. Speaking for myself, I may say that suggestion has no appeal. The suggestion has been made by Senator Mansfield to which reference was made by the Leader of the Opposition. Other suggestions have also been made.
Supply-External Affairs
I think the time has come when consideration might be given-and the United Nations might give consideration thereto-to the internationalizing of the city of Berlin under the United Nations, with its status to continue under United Nations presence. I realize that this suggestion would not receive the support of Mr. Khrushchev. However, it at least would bring about a step forward in the assurance that if negotiation failed, the United Nations would have something to which it could give its attention. It would require uncontrolled access by the west. It would also require a willingness on the part of the four powers to agree.
Someone has said that matters like this should not be discussed in advance of election campaigns in other parts of the world. I believe this is a serious enough matter that it should be discussed, if only for the purpose of directing the attention of mankind to a possible solution before it becomes too late to do so. As I said in Winnipeg and now repeat, Canada being one of the smaller nations, a member of NATO and of NORAD, with its record of sacrifice it has a right and a responsibility to place its views before mankind. After all, if the decision is left to four nations, without any suggestions having come from the smaller nations, the moral responsibility will rest on the governments of the smaller nations for having failed to advance their views.
There is one thing I wish to point out. I read that one of the pundits said that in the course of my Winnipeg speech I had not revealed the points which would be subject to negotiation. I can only say that I have never known any success to be attained by revealing in advance of negotiations the stand you are going to take. However, that does not mean that the stand should not have been determined upon. That does not imply either that the government of Canada, in its desire for peace, has not made a number of important suggestions which, in the perspective of the future, can be revealed.
The possibility of developing a role for the United Nations as a means of achieving a solution to the Berlin problem must necessarily be carefully examined. In the past the United Nations has made notable contributions to the peaceful settlement of disputes.
In point of fact the potentialities of the United Nations in this connection have not been ignored. This suggestion on my part regarding the United Nations is not new. I would point out that on March 19, 1959, in answer to a question by the Leader of the Opposition in which he inquired of me whether I would give a report about the conversations that had just been completed with

Supply-External Affairs the Prime Minister and the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom, as found at page 2049 of Hansard of that year I stated as follows:
Our talks were largely in the nature of an exchange of information and a review of the German and Berlin problems and of the various proposals for a settlement of those problems now under study in western capitals and in NATO. I should emphasize that neither Mr. Macmillan nor I attempted to crystallize any British or Canadian position on specific questions under discussion. However, I might add that it is my belief that the United Nations might play some significant role in the solution of the Berlin problem, and that this phase deserves further and more careful study. I think it would be generally agreed that it was clear there was no essential difference in the British and Canadian assessments of the world situation or in the basic aims and policies of our two countries with regard to the complex questions of Germany, Berlin and European security.
I do not think I can add anything more to what I have said. I know the Leader of the Opposition, with his great experience in these matters, will realize that I can go no further than the outline I have just given the house.
At that time the Leader of the Opposition said this:
It is particularly gratifying to hear the Prime Minister say that there may be a way in which the United Nations can, in due course, play a part in this Berlin situation in a manner which would be helpful to peace and security.
Then, speaking in the house on April 7, 1959, as found at page 2294 of Hansard of that year, these words:
By way of contributing to this process of clarification Canada offered a few suggestions concerning the problem of Berlin.
That reference is to clarification of the joint NATO viewpoint arising from the NATO ministerial meeting which was then taking place in Washington and at which the then minister of national defence, Hon. George Pearkes, V.C., represented Canada. I continued:
In the Canadian view no agreement can be acceptable to the west which places in jeopardy the security of West Berlin otr the freedom of its citizens.
That view was expressed two and a half years ago. I continued:
It is also the Canadian view that the NATO countries could not accept a solution which might endanger the ties between the Federal Republic of Germany and the other countries of western Europe.
Since then from time to time representations have been made. Indeed, I might return to the words of General Pearkes when, reporting on the conference on April 8, 1959, he said this as reported at page 2344 of Hansard of that year:
It is unnecessary for me to elaborate on what the Prime Minister has said, though I would call attention to the statement he made about the suggestion which was advanced by the Canadian delegation that in some manner the United Nations might be able to assist in the solution of the Berlin problem.

Later he stated:
Further study has been given to the possibility of the United Nations playing some part, and suggestions were made at the meeting as to how the United Nations might contribute something to the solution of the problem. I pointed out that we in Canada were anxious that consideration be given to ways by which the present arrangements over Berlin could be strengthened, either by supplementary or substitute arrangements. I pointed out that the Prime Minister had made his statement as of March 19, and then I went on to say that I would doubt if the United Nations could play a useful part unless a four power agreement had first been reached. I suggested that a settlement involving the United Nations need not be weaker, and conceivably might be more stable, than the present position in which the powers are now in Berlin by right of conquest. Although the effective introduction of the United Nations into the Berlin situation could probably be accomplished only through the agreement of the four powers, it could serve to engage the interest of other governments in the freedom and independence of Berlin in a way which no agreement reached solely among the occupying powers could do. Accordingly I suggested it would be worth while for the permanent council to study the possibilities of a trole for the United Nations in the application of a solution to the Berlin problem, and an assurance was given that a full study would be made by the permanent council of the suggestions which were put forward.
I would also point out that there was an occasion when the United Nations did endeavour to be of some assistance in connection with Berlin, but it was not very successful. That had to do with the committee of the United Nations which was set up some 10 years ago.
On September 1, I stated: "The charter of the United Nations declares the primary purpose of the United Nations to be the maintenance of international peace and security. It must be ready to make use of the United Nations". As recognized by the hon. gentlemen speaking for the opposition, there are a number of complicating factors, not the least of which is the question of the timing of any United Nations involvement.
The United Nations could, to begin with, exercise the function of promoter of an agreement on the Berlin problem by providing a focus for world opinion, which could have the effect of impelling the powers directly concerned to settle their differences by negotiation. Second, the United Nations could, if the powers concerned could be persuaded to agree, act in various roles as observer to verify that any new agreement reached was being fully implemented in accordance with its provision. Third, the United Nations could be assigned the more difficult task of operating an international regime in Berlin.
The problem is one of selecting the role which is most likely to contribute to the settlement of the Berlin problem in particular circumstances. This means essentially that the role of the United Nations must be

related to developments in negotiations toward a settlement. The four powers have primary responsibility in Berlin, and must first enter into direct negotiations. There are some indications at the moment that there is a reasonable prospect of there being negotiations. When I speak of a reasonable prospect, I am not speaking in anticipation of possible success, in view of Mr. Khrushchev's intrinsic position. If direct negotiations succeed might there be a possibility of providing a role for the United Nations, perhaps as guarantor of the agreement reached.
It is important to remember that the effective introduction of the United Nations into Berlin could only be done by agreement of all the four powers. I need not say that this may not be easily achieved. Whatever the difficulty might be, I think the little powers and other nations to be affected by the outcome of the Berlin problem have a right to an opportunity to be heard and to place their views clearly before a forum of most of the nations on earth. Furthermore, I can think of the possibility of the United Nations role being that of an observer in the city, or a supervisor on the access routes. Consideration of this possibility might facilitate negotiations and, if the idea were implemented, it might provide a stabilizing element in what is bound to remain a sensitive area throughout the years.
Those in general are some of the suggestions that I place before the house in regard to this question. The particulars of others are so sensitive in detail, if I may use that word again, they cannot be brought before the house, much as I would like to do so.
I now come to something else. What should the United Nations do in the world today?
I listened to the hon. member for Oxford. He spoke with the authority of four years of representation of Canada, and effective represensation. I have heard it said that no member of any of the delegations had a wider acquaintanceship and friendship than he. He gave us something of a picture of the United Nations.

While we debate that stand in the interests of the maintenance of peace, Khrushchev continues to push forward inch by inch and mile by mile all over the world.

With regard to the other questions that have arisen, they will be answered in detail by the Secretary of State for External Affairs-As Prime Minister, I have always followed the course of not interfering with the ministers in the discharge of their responsibilities except that in regard to foreign policy I have followed the tradition of the United Kingdom, that the Prime Minister must take a particular interest in that field of national activity on which the safety of the state so largely depends.
If we could only plan internationally to' meet all of the changes of attitude and the circuitous courses followed by Mr. Khrushchev, things would be much simpler. The Leader of the Opposition asked whether there was any planning, any consultation regarding the sealing off, or any anticipation of the sealing off of ingress and egress between East Berlin and West Berlin. I frankly tell you I do not think that was anticipated. However-and I am. answering him in this regard-there is planning and consultation to cover potential emergencies as they may arise with respect to western rights and responsibilities in Berlin.
I cannot, of course, disclose what action NATO governments propose to take if the Soviet government or the East Germans attempt to-block off access to Berlin. It would, however, be a mistake to imply that on this vital matter western interests are dependent on improvisation at the time of or after the time of the event. The occupying powers, specifically the United States, the United Kingdom and France, have special responsibilities to ensure maintenance of access for their troops stationed in Berlin, and for their supplies. The Leader of the Opposition implied that there might be a tendency to wait upon events improvidently before deciding on courses of action. The United Kingdom, the United States and France are keeping the other members of NATO regularly informed of progress in their

planning against various contingencies which are seen as possibly arising over Berlin, and the government of Canada will continue to ensure that there is no slackening in the effectiveness of this consultation and planning.
This is no time for pessimism, Mr. Chairman. Equally it is not a time for optimism. Throughout the years all the free world has faced dire dangers. I remember in the fall of 1916 visiting the British House of Commons just prior to the change of administration and hearing the then prime minister, one of Britain's greatest, I think, the Right Hon. H. H. Asquith, say that they had passed through the gravest difficulties. A few weeks later I heard Lloyd George make his first speech as prime minister of the United Kingdom. I was one of seven Canadians who had that privilege. I might be asked how I happened to get into the gallery. As a matter of fact, Sir George Perley was on the troop ship returning to his job as high commissioner and he said that if at any time in the future there was anything I wanted I should get in touch with him. It was not many weeks before I did. I said, "I want a ticket to the gallery". He said, "That is a lot more difficult to secure than almost anything else you could ask for". I said, "That is what I want, that is what you promised me". I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, that is what I got.
I heard Lloyd George's speech and I have always remembered it. He had the power, the imagery and the command of language necessary for such an occasion. He compared the situation then to his boyhood days when he used to look toward the west with a mountain immediately in front of him. He wondered what was beyond that mountain so finally he climbed it and there was another mountain ahead. He said, "I knew that somewhere beyond there was hope for the world". I believe that today. I believe that if the free world will but stand firm, resolute and determined and at the same time not stubbornly unresilient to the necessities that are brought about through change, we shall come out of the Berlin problem stronger in the things of the spirit than ever before; for, as I see it, if we follow a course of defeatism by giving up our principles, we shall have laid the foundations for a future frightful to contemplate.
Communism does not understand any other principle than power. Communism does not believe in an immortal being who determines the course of mankind, even though sometimes taking generations to do so. We do, and if we do our part now without permitting ourselves to be intimidated I think there is a possibility that we shall be laying the foundations for a new relationship between the communist world and the world of freedom,
Supply-External Affairs a relationship which cannot be hoped to be attained if we capitulate to the degree Khrushchev asks us to. If we give up our principles, what have we to live for in the years ahead?
I remember that in the dark days of 1917 Quiller-Couch wrote a novel about two men who opposed one another, one of whom believed in the things of the spirit and the other of whom ridiculed such beliefs. The one who believed in the things of the spirit gave up his principles in order to defeat his opponent. He did. He won and when he had achieved victory there was no difference between him in his victory and his opponent if he had been successful.
I know there are some who say that they think the things of the spirit should not be considered. We are right in the stand we are taking in this matter. It is not only a question of the people of West Berlin although we gave our pledge there and must keep it. It is a question of whether we shall allow Khrushchev with intimidation and threats to push us back and back to a point where we have nothing but our past to look back on. If there is to be a future, if mankind is going forward to higher and better things, the things of the spirit are as important to nations as they are to individuals. It is in that spirit that I hope the free world will stand, prepared to make those changes which the realities demand but not prepared to sacrifice the principle in which we believe, the principle of the right of people to live under law even though the rule of law is not effective internationally.

First, the hon. member for Greenwood mentioned coexistence.
I thought the hon. member for Greenwood made an excellent speech.
It is a peculiarity of the thinking today, in the United States particularly, that to mention the word "coexistence" puts one sort of into the appeasement class or that of a fellow traveller. There is more than that. There is no doubt that they have the solid support of a large segment of their population. They are going to remain there unless they can be overthrown by force of arms and, as I

said before. I think that any question of overthrow by force of arms means we will be out of the frying pan and into the fire. It cannot be done without destroying us all.
Therefore peaceful coexistence is the only existence there is. It is not an alternate form of action; it is the only possibility. Therefore we must do all we can to try to relieve the tension which might destroy us all. Certainly if we are going to live in peace with our neighbours it would behoove us to have a foreign policy more in keeping with our Christian, democratic principles than merely an anti-communist line.
I thought the hon. member made a very courageous speech on that occasion. I should like to quote from an editorial in the August 29 issue of the Vancouver Sun. It is entitled, "The Dreams and the Facts."
"We are in an impossible situation over Berlin and our refusal of de facto recognition to east Germany is a position we shall have to abandon sooner or later."
Dr. Hugh Keenleyside said it. It would have sounded even better in the mouths of some western statesmen who permit themselves only to think it.
In public, spokesmen of the west still pay lip service to daydreams. Daydreams are more pleasant than facts, but not as useful in diplomatic bargaining.
One dream: Russia will permit free elections which would result in East Germany joining the west.
The fact: Russia won't give it up. She fears a reunited Germany. So do many people of the western world.
Dream: We shall pretend the east German state isn't there. Perhaps it will wither away.
Fact: The puppet state can be kept alive by Russia as long as she feels she needs it. Since we have rearmed West Germany, that is likely to be a long time.
Dream: All that is necessary is that the west show a united front in West Berlin.
Fact: It is a poor place for a front line. It is a western island more than 100 miles inside the Russian empire. Military experts say it is indefensible.
Dream: Khrushchev wouldn't dare start a war.
Fact: Khrushchev doesn't need to. He plans to sign a peace treaty, 16 years delayed, and give East Germany control of the West Berlin access routes.
Dream: We can fight our way in.
Fact: No one has shown how, except by launching a nuclear war which would result in certain destruction of Russia and the United States and perhaps everybody else too.

Mr. Chairman, it was a great
privilege for me to hear the speech made by the Prime Minister to the bar association in Winnipeg, the theme of which was that the fullest discussion and negotiation must take place before we can have any thought of war. I feel very humble today in speaking after the very great address given by the Prime Minister. However, I have always taken an interest in international affairs and in my maiden speech on May 29 I referred to this part of the speech from the throne:
My government will continue to make unremitting efforts to assist the peaceful solution of international problems and in the accomplishment by patient negotiation of a substantial measure of disarmament.
In referring to that passage I quoted a report appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of May 15 under the headline "Montgomery Feels Canada Should Lead Free Crusade".
I quote from that report:
It seems to me Canada is in a unique position to provide robust world leadership. Your nation

Supply-External Affairs cannot be charged with the stigma of colonialism; you're lucky that way. You have a very good amalgam of French and British blood; that's good.
It is quite clear to me that the nations of the world are looking to Canada for a lead. That is a fact. I am not saying that to please you. I would like to see Canada develop a foreign policy of its own, not tacked on to someone else, and give that lead.
I believe Montgomery is a man of great experience. He is a man who knows about wars and he is a lover of peace. He has taken an independent attitude on world problems and Canada might very well heed his advice.
I was very much touched by the reference made by the Prime Minister to our great Secretary of State for External Affairs, who has devoted so much of his time toward the maintenance of peace and disarmament. However, the Prime Minister stated about our worthy Secretary of State for External Affairs that in the opinion of the Kremlin his work showed weakness, instead of greatness. I think the battle for peace and disarmament is not ended; it must be sustained, and the more so when the need is greater.
Napoleon once said

and he was a man of war, as everyone knows-that even in war moral power is to physical as to three parts out of four.
Mahatma Gandhi relied only on moral power and he was able to obtain, by his passive resistance, the freedom and independence of India. Nehru today has nothing more than moral power to offer the world, yet both the west and the communists are competing for his approval and are shrinking from his disapproval.
As I said before, it was a great privilege for me to hear the speech made by the Right Hon. Prime Minister to the Canadian Bar Association on September 1.1 feel that Canada should never be committed to war by proxy. The key to our participation should never be left to those who dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima or Nagasaki. Canadians want Canada to be free, not a mere appendage to our southern neighbour. Canadians have faith in the logic and humanity of our Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs. We cannot give a proxy to either NATO or NORAD. We cannot abdicate our right in advance to keep us from maintaining or breaking the peace.
I should like to quote a few proverbs and sayings in connection with war. Franklin said:
There never was a good war, or a bad peace.
General Grant of the United States said:
When wars do come, they fall upon the many, the producing class, who are the sufferers.
There is a German proverb which says:
A great war leaves the country with three armies-an army of cripples, an army of mourners and an army of thieves.

Wellington said:
Men who have nice notions of religion have no business to be soldiers.
Wellington also said:
The next dreadful thing to a battle lost is a battle won.
Fielding said:
War is the sink of all injustice.
Tertullian said:
In disarming Peter, Christ disarmed every soldier.
We are presently suffering from a recurrent attack of war virus. This virus thrives on the thirst for conquest, thirst for turmoil and the innate ferocity and barbarism of man. Any student of history well knows that all wars have been futile in their results. I well recall in 1940 listening to a lecture by a professor of history at the University of Manitoba, Professor R. O. MacFarlane. He was also chairman of the royal commission on education in Manitoba and gave very great service in this respect. He stated at the time we were at war with Germany that after the war we would become the allies of Germany in a war against Russia.
This is what happened. Probably 20 years from now we may be allied with Russia in a war against China. If we could get all our scientists to study the history of mankind from the very beginning, I think they could through the use of computing machines, tell us the date of the next war. In my opinion, this is how human nature works. It is like that of the lemmings which periodically go and jump in the sea, driven by we do not know what. It seems to me that human nature is almost the same and that war will come. It is said that war is unthinkable, but I believe it is possible and I believe that we should really prepare for it.
How futile was the bloodshed in the past when one considers that the nation we have bombed and whose nationals we have killed by the thousands is our best friend today and that the nation we helped to defend is our deadly enemy today. How futile was our participation in such carnage when we realize that the avowed object of our participation was the defence of Poland and that one of the first provisions of the peace treaty provided for the enslavement of Poland. How naive were the leaders of the world who made the peace that divided the city of Berlin one half of it free and one half of it enslaved. Wars breed more wars. We won the war but we lost the peace.
The war spirit is a disease of the mind and of the heart caused by the lack of the love of God and the abandonment of Christian principles. The lesson of history teaches us

that today's friends will be tomorrow's enemies and that our objective of today will be altered tomorrow and perhaps be completely reversed. One should never be the aggressor, no matter what the provocation. No loss of prestige or, as the orientals say, loss of face, can be a sufficient reason to go to war. If we went to war for Berlin, Berlin would be destroyed and therefore the purpose would be non-existent. If we go to war, no matter what we do, history will show that we did not settle the question on Berlin.
I do not wish to leave the impression that I am opposed to war preparations because the old saying of the Romans si vis pacem, para bellum has always been true. I know that we must prepare for our defence. When I say that, I like to think of what was told to Canada at one time-it was on August 31, 1955-namely that there were two fronts to defend, the military front and the home front. We have acquitted ourselves very well with regard to that part that dealt with the military front but only now are we going to do something worth while for the home front. I scrapped a couple of pages of my speech because I was going to be very severe with the Liberal party. When I came to this house in 1958 and questioned the then minister of national health and welfare, he told me that under the Liberal regime they had prepared for a million casualties but they neglected to do anything to prevent those casualties. Either they wanted to justify the expense by not providing for doing away with casualties or they wanted to encourage some of their business friends by buying a great deal of material. At least it showed that they expected that it was possible to have a million casualties. I think there is no excuse for having done nothing about civil defence. I should like to express my great satisfaction in the announcement that we are going to train 100,000 men by groups of 25,000. I think this is a very good beginning. I want to reserve my comments until I get the full details of this organization. I have here the August number of a book called Pageant. In it there is an article entitled "Inside Russian Civil Defence". It took five years for Khrushchev who started that activity himself when he took power in 1955, the time when we were told that the time to act was now. I understand the civil defence organization was completed in Russia in 1960. Instead of commenting I am going to read this article fully. It is found at page 6 and is by Henry Jordan. He says this:
Our program has been muddled, and our attitude fatalistic. But the Soviets give every citizen years of intensive training. Should we be doing likewise? Here is the first, complete report on the little known Red plan for survival.
