Do you know what "fallout" is made of? Why it spreads? How to gauge the "delay period" after a nuclear bomb burst-the time it's still safe to be outdoors?
Do you know what kind of clothing will fully protect you against residual radiation? Or how to rid your kitchen utensils easily of dangerous radioactivity?
Being unable to answer these and other such questions makes you a definite risk in the age of nucleonics. But. as you are no doubt aware, you're in a vast and mostly excellent company: perhaps 98 per cent of us in these 50 states.
You may not consider knowing the answers to these questions of very much importance to your life. You, along with most Americans, may consider all civil defence activity a hopeless exercise in futility. We have been told by various philosophers, statesmen and some scientists that a nuclear war would finish our civilization if not life itself, turning this world into a ball of poisonous ashes-a cosmic monument to man's folly-no matter what our precautions or preparations.
Perhaps so. But it may surprise you to know that a few thousand miles away in the Soviet union every factory worker, high school senior, subway conductor, plant manager and housewife is able to answer the questions cited in his sleep- and many more besides.
As our intelligence men know only too well, all Soviet citizens from 16 to 60-upwards of 135 million people-have six years of the stiffest civil defense drill behind them. With only the bedridden and insane excepted, they were required to attend classes and were taken out on field exercises to learn in theory and practice how to survive war in the age of the fiery mushroom cloud and radioactive fallout.
The leaders in the Kremlin obviously hope that our interest in civil defence will continue to be desultory, that most of us will continue to believe -despite governmental exhortations-that we cannot survive a nuclear war. Soviet Premier Khrushchev himself has repeatedly uttered gloomy predictions that a war of rocket-propelled H-bombs would leave no victor, only total destruction.
But there are experts who warn that Khrushchev is no more sincere than Henry L. Menckens mournful undertaker "conducting a $900 funeral." He would not draft every man, woman and halfchild for army-type drills every 12 or 18 months, spend badly needed funds, manpower and materials on anti-nuclear shelters, anti-fallout masks and decontamination equipment, unless he considered the "unthinkable" war a possibility after all-and that measures could be taken to reduce the toll.
What is the exact nature of Soviet civil defence preparations? Is there anything we can learn from them? Should we be taking similar steps?
On the following pages, Pageant presents the first comprehensive report on Soviet civil defence ever put before the American public. The information comes from many sources-secret Soviet training manuals, military periodicals, intelligence reports, interviews with escapees.
What emerges is a picture of a nation systematically being readied for the ultimate horror of a nuclear war. The story may well shock many Americans out of their business as usual mood. It contains information vital to an understanding of the basic political battle of our times.
Probably nothing characterizes DOSAFF, the Soviet civil defence organization, more tellingly than the fact that all its activities are classified defence secrets. (The initials stand for Dobrovolnoe Obshchestvo Sodeistviia Armii, Aviatsii i Flotu or: "Volunteer Society for Assistance to Army, Air Force and Navy.") Appropriately, DOSAAF was in the administrative grip of the Soviet secret police until 1958, when an organizational shuffle put it

Supply-External Affairs under the Ministry of Internal Affairs. But experts on Soviet affairs point out that the shift changed nothing-95 per cent of the Ministry's work concerns secret police activities.
Informed observers believe there are two major reasons for the secrecy surrounding Russian civil defence. First, the Soviet leaders do not wish to alarm other countries into setting up similar survival programs. Second, they do not want anyone to draw the conclusion that the Soviet preparedness drive could mean planning for war, not peace.
Yet it was Khrushchev himself who violated the secrecy rule a few years ago. Then he boasted to a German newsman of how formidable the Soviet union was, and how her rockets would obliterate all enemies without great cost to the Russian people, who were made safe from nuclear horrors by the largest civil defence program in the world.
"After I took over, I brought up the cadres of permanent civil defence workers to twenty two million, most of them demobilized army personnel," Khrushchev declared. And this was not an unlikely figure, considering that in World War II DOSAAF's hard core, recruited from a far smaller population, was made up of 25 million people.
The reactivation of DOSAAF Khrushchev spoke about goes back to 1955, when he succeeded Georgi Malenkov as actual head of the Soviet state. Surely a thermonuclear war would be costly, reasoned Khrushchev. But with sufficient preparation on the civil defence front, Russia's losses could be minimized, while the overconfident Western world would be effectively destroyed.
Civil defence therefore headed the list of Khrushchev's new projects. He ordered an immediate "mass attack"-the popular Soviet term for crash program. Within a few weeks, of his assuming power, directives were issued and Russian adults and adolescents of both sexes-by Soviet count, 83 per cent of the population-"volunteered" for DOSAAF civil defence courses.
Simultaneously, millions of training pamphlets were turned out. They dealt with the nuclear facts of life-gamma rays, "thermal storm," and what could be learned from observation of the fireball and mushroom cloud of H-bomb blasts.
The training courses of 1955, the first of several, ran ten class hours mainly devoted to theory. This was supplemented by field exercises in decontamination and first aid held on week ends and Sundays, the number depending on local needs.
At the conclusion of the course, each trainee was required to appear before a board and take a stiff exam on his knowledge of civil defence procedures. Low marks resulted in a return to class for further training. High marks earned DOSAAF's students certificates, brass badges, and hints of job promotion.
Whatever other ends the DOSAAF drills served, they helped strip atomic war of some of its awesomeness. General Boris Olisov, commander of the Red Army's Corps of Engineers, made a revealing comment about this in the usual upside-down Kremlin fashion:
"The western imperialists keep magnifying the danger of nuclear war", he wrote in Red Star the Soviet Army newspaper. "Their plan is to frighten, bully and blackmail other nations into submission. But this will get them nowhere as far as the Soviet goes. Her people have lost all fear of nuclear attack, thanks to systematic training in all aspects of civil defence".
Elsewhere in the article, the general hinted about the nature of future DOSAAF drills.
"You can't get to know all about civil defence in one day or one course. Yet, as our trainees are finding out, the simple, old fashioned rules hold true even in this age. Jumping into a ditch raises

a man's chances to outlive a nuclear blast ten times. A ditch is still man's best friend."
What did the millions of DOSAAF students learn?
I interviewed a former trainee who had escaped to the west.
First of all, he revealed, the hazards of nuclear war were consistently minimized-often sensibly so. Fallout, the DOSAAF teachers lectured is literally "trash"-dust and debris. When one of the big bombs goes off, a violent updraft sucks tons of liquefied, vaporized earth, stone and metal skyward to heights of 100 thousand feet and more. This debris is "hot"-highly radioactive.
Rather quickly, the vapors and droplets solidify in the thin, cold air of the upper atmosphere and "fall out". While they are still tumbling downward like myriad specks of dust, the ground, even in the immediate blast area, is entirely free of radioactivity.
This is a last, desperate period of grace during which it is still safe to leave shelter, gather up one's family, fight fires, or give and get medical attention.
Depending on weather and wind, the period of "dead time" may last 50 minutes or eight hours. Then, when the first fallout fragments set Geiger counters clicking, people will take cover.
"Even a roof of cardboard can save your life," the DOSAAF textbook informed students. "But just as radioactive dust must be prevented from touching your skin, it also has to be kept out of your lungs. The cheapest face mask equipped with a cloth filter will do an adequate job. If you have no mask, breathe through a damp handkerchief.
In a further attempt to take the terror out of nuclear war, DOSAAF training put great emphasis on the fact that fallout is as perishable as a snowflake in the hot sun. Scientifically this is entirely correct. Ten hours after a bomb burst, all the rampaging, life-destroying radioactivity loses 90 per cent of its strength. Before two weeks are up, life in a city can gradually resume, since radiation by then will be down to one tenth of 1 per cent.
Advanced Course
In 1956, at the close of the short Russian summer, DOSAAF again beat the drums to call all citizens for a second round of survival lessons. Classes started without delay. This time the emphasis was on practical matters, like Olisov's ditches.
Millions of citizens drilled in practice digging. They set fire to huge trash piles and put them out again, timed by instructors' stopwatches. To limber up still further, they were taken, regardless of health, on 20-mile marches, so-called "exercises in emergency evacuation."
Evening classes tackled "how to" matters: How to keep food and water supplies from absorbing poisonous radioactivity, for example (by sealing out dust). How to rid kitchen utensils of dangerous radioactivity (by washing with soap and water). How to rid oneself of "hot" fallout (by washing and more washing).
In the vast Russian hinterlands, DOSAAF instructors stressed problems of the sod and barn.
With animals, by and large, they told students, proceed as with humans. Make sure they are under cover when fallout starts. If radioactive matter gets on their hides, scrub them with soap and water. Should their eyes turn red-irritated from looking at the bomb's fireball-rinse them with DOSAAF's special eyewash.
What if the earth itself gets a dose of ionizing poison? Wait for rain to settle the dust. Then plow the hot trash under. Chances are it won't bother you again. Each rainfall will wash the hot debris deeper while time scatters its radioactivity.
The second DOSAAF training course also covered weapons not mentioned before: poison gas and bacterial warfare.

Instructors lectured about plagues, pests, infected lice, bacillus-derived botulism toxin (so powerful that a thimbleful could make New York City's entire water supply too deadly to drink), and how to detect germs by use of a biological detector kit. Poison gases were dealt with just as thoroughly -how the various kinds act, how to identify them, what protection is available, how to give first aid and how to de-gas a building.

At the end of the second course-a total of 22 class hours and much field work-the final exam was supplemented with a practical experiment to
Supply-External Affairs emphasize the lessons learned. Every trainee was forced to spend 30 minutes in a room filled with chloropicrin, a lethal world war I gas that has a habit of penetrating seemingly tight masks.
Children Too
A third DOSAAF course started in mid-1959 and lasted into 1960. It required 14 class hours and again a locally determined number of week ends and Sunday sessions. The scope of its curriculum is reflected in the variety of questions students were asked in the final examinations. To mention only a few:
"What are the effects of 125 roentgen units of radiation on unprotected people (a) after one hour; (b) after 12 hours?
How do you put a breathing mask on a wounded person in 30 seconds?
What medical self-help procedures are available in case of (a) atomic, (b) gas, or (c) germ attack?"
Trainees able to answer 80 such questions received a somewhat cryptically inscribed badge: "Study in Air Defence."
The DOSAAF program does not forget children. They, too, have training to undergo. From the age of six they were required to attend lectures that told them of death rays you can't see or feel; insects that spread plagues; Geiger counters; how to tie on a gas mask; what to do when (a) one parent or (b) both parents are killed. Children who knew their lessons well were awarded shiny brass buttons with the imprint "Ready for Defence."
Concrete Mathematics
The ability to live through a nuclear conflict is not only a matter of knowledge. The Russians are well aware that it is a matter of solid radiation-proof shelters also.
As intelligence sources have pointed out, an entire government city has been under construction for some years seven miles from Moscow. It is now being rushed to completion. Hacked out of primeval rock, this emergency Kremlin is buried 1300 feet below ground level. It is designed to take a direct hit by a 20-megaton hydrogen bomb-the equivalent of 20 million pounds of t.n.t. Stores food, fuel and oxygen will be large enough to last through a two-year siege.
Thousands of smaller shelters are now being readied throughout the country-shelters calculated to take anything but a direct hit. There are also the deep subways of Moscow, Kiev, and Leningrad, designed years ago as bomb shelters as well as transport facilities. And a law passed in the 1930's made it mandatory to equip every new building, small family dwellings included, with bomb shelters of steel-reinforced concrete.
Obviously there is some civic delusion in this pretense that any kind of shelter could be a match for H-bombs. But basically, the leaders in the Kiemlin are as exact in their calculations as business machines.
Stripped of essentials, Soviet survival mathematics go like this: In a war, 50 to 100 nuclear bombs will drop on Russian soil. Where they hit, shelters will be smashed, all life extinct.
But immediately outside the impact area and beyond it, thousands of shelters will be intact, and, provided fallout precautions are taken, people will survive.
This viewpoint, of course, is no Soviet exclusive. It is shared by many American experts, and by organizations which have carried out critical surveys of this country's defence postures in recent years. Among them are the collective authors of the Rockefeller, Gaither, Johns Hopkins and the National Academy of Sciences reports, which called for an immediate crash program in shelter construction.

Supply-External Affairs
But while our "reports" gathered dust and we did little or nothing, the purposeful men in the Kremlin pushed the construction of shelters for all. By the end of 1960, intelligence sources inform us, the program was completed-one U.S. expert called it the most extensive shelter program in the world.
And now that every Soviet town and crossroads had its shelter, DOSAAF in early spring of 1961 launched still another ambitious drill program, billed as "exercises in shelter management."
The typical Soviet big-city shelter, with a capacity of 2000 persons, is a mass of steel and concrete set deep underground. It is equipped with blastproof steel doors, emergency exit tunnels, airfiltering apparatus, its own water and power systems, detection devices for radiation, gases, and microbes, and enough food and compressed oxygen to last two weeks, the time necessary for radioactivity to drop to tolerable levels.
These shelters are engineered to withstand a nuclear bomb burst a few blocks away. Shelters in places unlikely to come under direct attack offer proportionately less elaborate protection. Those in rural areas, where fallout is the only worry, are little more than dugouts lined with lumber and roofed over with tin or scrap lumber.
"Two feet of dirt piled on the roof," DOSAAF instructors tell their classes, "will filter out 99 per cent of the fallout radiation."
A parallel features of the present drill is "evacuation exercises," and thereby hangs an interesting Soviet policy reversal.
All through the years, implacable regulations had called for city populations to stay put in case of war, allowing for certain exceptions.
But under recently decreed rules, only essential manpower stays behind. The vast majority- perhaps because of improved transportation-will be evacuated, first to staging areas 25 to 50 miles beyond city limits, then to Russia's vast, safe back country, along routes dotted with fallout-proof way stations.
In an atomic war, shelters or not, the dead in Russia would pile up. Estimates on the probable extent of the casualties are available. Last year, a Soviet military attache, toasting his way through a diplomatic dinner in Paris, let slip what he said was the Red Army's guess: two million dead.
"A bargain," he added. "During World War II we lost twenty five million."
Off-the-record American computations of Soviet losses, based on the probable numbers of targets and bombs involved, are remarkably close to the talkative Soviet official's two million.
But what would American losses be? Based on the current state of our civil defence preparations, if war came tomorrow our casualties would be 62 million dead and 24 million wounded.
The statistics of this carnage represent the result of dispassionate calculations by some of our best qualified experts. In the summer of 1959, the blood-chilling estimates were submitted at congressional committee hearings called by Representative Chet Holifield of California.
The official reaction was silence-tantamount, in the view of some observers, to an endorsement of the estimates and a tacit acknowledgment that one half of the nation would be maimed or slaughtered in any future atomic war.
The official Soviet position could be summed up like this: A well-informed, properly trained people who know the worst and the best about a disaster situation are not likely to lapse into hysteria and self-pitying thoughts of doom and surrender, or even simple resignation to fate.
Khrushchev must have had this in mind when a few years ago he commented with blunt cynicism: "A nuclear war will drive the capitalist popu-

lation into insanity. Only the people in the communist countries will hold up well. They know what to expect and are fully prepared for it."
To "prepare" us, we have our own "DOSAAF," in the OCDM-office of civil defence mobilization- headed by director Frank B. Ellis and forming part of the executive office of the president.
Unlike DOSAAF, OCDM has been accused of being in a state of suspended animation from the start. Critics have claimed that it dozed through one cold war crisis after another, and that it was not even shaken up by the roaring fireball which leapt into the Siberian sky on August 12, 1953, heralding the birth of the Soviet H-bomb.
Coupled with official lethargy, of course, has been that of the American citizen. Attempts to arouse him to support of a civil defence system have met with almost universal failure. Part of the trouble, too, is that officials have admitted both publicly and privately that our defence program is inadequate.
Director Ellis of the OCDM as late as last April characterized the American civil defence program as "completely inadequate". Ellis pressed a demand for a program almost tripled in size-and emphasized his seriousness by threatening to resign if funds for the expansion were not forthcoming. He was opposed by both the director of the budget and the president's special assistant for national security affairs; other administration projects, they said, had greater priority for funds.
The Kremlin, however, is never in doubt as to the day and age we live in and plows industriously ahead with large-scale, costly defence plans. Their reasoning seems to be that "the bomb" is here to stay, something to live with, and if possible to survive.
DOSAAF promises its students that they will be able to straighten out a radioactive city in no time at all. Streets, roofs, and house walls will be cleansed of radioactivity by teams with fire hoses. Since fallout is only dust made radioactive, decontamination of dwellings will amount to little more than a thorough spring cleaning. Soviet citizens are told they should do the job in tight clothing, gloves and breathing masks.
Order. I wonder whether the hon. member could indicate how much more he has.

I believe I have three or four short paragraphs. I am sorry to inflict this punishment on the committee but I think it is very important to publicize civil defence in general.
When they are done with the job, the efficient DOSAAF will pick up the clothing and wash it free of radiation in one of its decontamination laundries.
Eyewash for Ivan? Is it really all that simple and innocuous?
No, it certainly isn't. DOSAAF glosses over many difficulties, but that is only customary with patriotic literature. Yet it is an undeniable fact that DOSAAF's relaxed views on fallout are shared by many American and British experts.
In some instances, the agreement is word for word. Some official DOSAAF publications are simply plagiarized versions of western works.
The works of Dr. Willard F. Libby, Nobel prize winner, former member of the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission and a prolific writer on the atom, have been repeatedly pirated by the Russians.
No friend of the Soviets and an unwilling DOSAAF author, Dr. Libby nevertheless shares DOSAAF's views on fallout. Time and time again he has stated in scientific periodicals and before

congressional committees that what some have said of the danger of fallout is immensely exaggerated.
More than 160 bombs-both atomic and hydrogen, Including some of the largest and "dirtiest"- were set off between 1945 and 1958. Yet, as Dr. Lloyd W. Law of the national cancer institute told a congressional committee, the resulting fallout "was no more likely to produce cancer than two cigarettes a year".
For wearers of watches with luminous dials, Dr. Libby pointed out an interesting comparison: The radiation received from such a watch dial amounts to 40 units a year-as against one unit from thermonuclear bursts in an average year of testing.
That is the end of the article. I wish to thank the committee for putting up with my reading of this long article. I did not finish more than about one third of my speech but as I understand I can speak twice I will take a breathing spell and I may continue after another member has spoken. It took five years for Russia to complete its civil defence program. I should like to compliment the government for starting what one might call a crash program in civil defence and I think we will need all of five years with an accelerated program.

In his speech the other day the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not touch on the situation in Laos. In view of the importance of this situation in the context of current international problems confronting us, and as Canada is a member of the reactivated international truce commission in Laos, I am sure that the committee will expect a statement from the minister with regard to the situation in that turbulent little country.
When we last met in this house in regard to matters on which the minister had an opportunity to make some comment, he was about to leave for the Geneva conference. Since that time the conference has met from time to time, and in so far as one can judge from what has transpired, no real progress has been made. The minister had taken a proper position with regard to supplying the commission with equipment essential for the prosecution of the assignment given to the commission, of which Canada is a member. We would like to have from the minister a report as to whether or not it has been given the kind of assistance, the necessary equipment, to enable it to discharge its functions properly.
The more fundamental question as to whether there has been an effective cease fire is another matter about which I think the committee would expect a report. Then, there is the still more important question of whether or not the conference is going to be able to achieve the purpose hoped for by the United States, the United Kingdom and other countries, namely, a truly independent and neutral government. Not much progress on that point seems to have been made. I noticed the other day that the vice premier of communist China, or perhaps it was Mr. Chou En-lai himself, who seemed to indicate that it was ridiculous to assume that in Laos there could be a truly independent neutral government. He indicated rather there would be a government that would express the wishes of the people, and that the consequence would be that it would be a government made up of individuals who did not support the position of the west, who did not really maintain a neutral position, but were closer to the communist orbit than any other.
In any event, this conference that is taking place does not give me, at least, any particular confidence in its outcome, although I would hope that the situation were otherwise. This problem of Laos has been with us for some time. It certainly has taken an aggravated form within the period of the last eight months, although ever since the Geneva accord of 1954 it has been a problem of concern not only to the United States

Supply-External Affairs but to all peace loving countries. One would wish that the west had shown the same foresight as hindsight, because what had been urged upon the United States in 1956 is now accepted by that country as the kind of condition it would like to see prevail. It is regrettable that that position could not have been taken earlier. In this particular instance, it is only right to say that strong representations were made by western countries, including Canada, as to what was the wisest course to take in Laos.
We cannot forgo the view that, just as Berlin is now engaging our attention, once that problem is resolved we might find tur-bulency and a critical situation developing in a new form in Laos. Now that we have an opportunity to review what is being done at the conference in Geneva, it would be well for us to anticipate in every way possible an arrangement that would avoid the kind of situation which could eventuate, that is another crisis on which the communist world would be prepared to hang its hat. We know of the infiltration that is going on from North Viet Nam under the direction of Ho Chi Minh, and the kind of obstruction that is coming from another communist area in Asia.
This is a situation in which we have an interest, as one of the nations. It is one that engages our specific interest because we are a member of the international truce commission. I would be grateful to the minister, as I am sure the committee would be, for an up to date report as to what is happening in Geneva. What is the situation with regard to discharging our role in accordance with our mandate as a member of the commission?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the situation with regard to Laos is not as bad as the hon. member for Essex East has indicated, although one would be foolish to predict just what is going to happen. For example, I believe the monsoon season is now drawing to a close and the result may be an increase in military activity. The presence of the truce supervisory commission, of which India is chairman and Poland and Canada are members, has helped considerably to keep to a minimum the conflict in that unfortunate country.
Mind you, the commission has not yet received adequate equipment. There have been offers made, for example, recently by the royal government side and that particular picture is not as bad as it was a few weeks ago. I think the communists would like to see the commission have as little power and be just as ineffective as possible. On the other hand, throughout, we have taken the position that the commission had a job to do and that it should be given the tools with

which to do that job. It has been impossible for the commission to visit any spot where there has been actual fighting or which could be described as a danger spot. However, representatives of the three parties in Laos are meeting quite regularly. Sometimes the commission is allowed to sit in; sometimes it is not allowed to do so.
There seems to be a great deal of patience exercised on all sides. The hon. member, from his experience in the Orient, will agree there is not much use trying to be in a big hurry in that part of the world. Patience is one of the main requisites to getting along.
I have the utmost admiration for the way in which the Canadians on this commission have been functioning in Laos. We have about 26 officers and men from the Department of National Defence and eight or 10 from the Department of External Affairs under Mr. May-rand, who is our ambassador to Italy. I have been very pleased with the job they have done under most trying conditions. Canada in that part of the world is making a splendid contribution.
In Geneva, in the meantime, the 14-nation conference is working on a declaration of neutrality for Laos and on a pact which will establish the proper controls. For example, it will deal with getting outside fighting troops away from the country, the importation of arms, and that sort of thing. They have practically agreed upon a declaration of neutrality and are now working on the other document, which will be longer and a great deal more difficult to conclude.
The hon. member should not feel that progress is not being made. I should be very reluctant myself to be sitting in Geneva participating in all these discussions, because there have been a great many of them and there has been a tremendous amount of frustration. But Mr. Chester Ronning, our high commissioner in India, Mr. Paul Bridle, our ambassador to Turkey, and Brigadier Leech of the Department of National Defence, have been carrying on there day after day and week after week and considerable progress has been made.
I am hopeful it will be possible within the next few weeks for the 14-nation conference to reach agreement with regard to Laos. I cannot guarantee that will be the result, because the whole question may blow up. But there is considerable hope that a settlement will be reached. If that is the case, this may be the first field in which something worth while has been accomplished for the last many months.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is optimistic as to the possible conclusion of the conference that is under

way in Geneva. I do not wish to say much more about the situation in Laos except that I feel the minister's optimism, understandable though it is, nevertheless is not a realistic appreciation of the situation in that sector.
Of course the minister has an advantage that I do not possess. He is aware of the latest exchanges and the nature of all the discussions in Geneva. But it seems to me we ought to take a very realistic view of what is happening in the whole of Indo-China. While there may be a declaration of agreement on the question of the kind of neutrality that is to prevail regarding government in Laos, it would surprise me very much, in view of the record there and the infiltrations that are taking place via North Viet Nam and from across the Chinese-Burma border, if we can conclude that there have as yet been placed before us those guarantees which would give us the conviction that the solemn undertaking of those ideologically opposed to us will be observed. However, only time will tell.
The situation in Laos is not unrelated to what is taking place in South Viet Nam particularly. I take it that the truce commission continues to operate in Cambodia. While perhaps there is no great expense involved in the maintenance of the international truce commission in Cambodia, some justification ought to be given for its continuance. I am not saying it should not be continued, but when we talk of Cambodia we cannot overlook the forebodings of the former head of the government, Prince Sihanouk, who I believe has since resigned, repeating what he has done on other occasions. His apprehension as to what is likely to eventuate from the kind of discussions that have taken place in Geneva indicate that this is a theatre in which we could have increasing trouble in the future.
We hope this will be avoided, but in our survey of what is going on in the world it seems most desirable that we should at least have some idea of the dangers that lurk in that sector, not only because of its effect in Cambodia, Laos and North Viet Nam, but because of the ultimate consequences throughout southeast Asia.
One can very well see what would happen if by a process of attrition Laos were to go by the board. Then Cambodia might go and there would be an increasing strain upon the kind of defence that South Viet Nam would be able to put up against the forces of Ho Chi Minh. Then the consequences for Thailand and ultimately for other Asian countries like India are all part of the process which we must inevitably take into account in the kind of world in which we are living. Supply-External Affairs minister wish to say anything about the truce commission, particularly in North Viet Nam?
The United States government has apparently been able to satisfy President Diem of its intention to increase its assistance to that country in various forms. What does this further assistance mean in terms of further obligations on the part of the international truce commission? Is there any prospect whatsoever of the truce commission in this country being called upon to liquidate its operation in the foreseeable future? I am not advising that; I am merely inquiring. I ask this question because I feel, as I am sure the minister does, that this is one of those areas where we can anticipate an increase in responsibility and concern.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Essex East is unduly pessimistic.
Realistic.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He speaks of South Viet Nam falling, Cambodia falling, Laos falling, Thailand falling, Burma and India falling. They may. I cannot guarantee that they will not. But if I were foreign minister of the Soviet union I think I could record a much longer list of countries in which the Soviet union is not doing so well and where they should be shedding a lot of tears.
In my judgment, on the western side there is too much inferiority complex about the Russians; that they are always outsmarting us and we are always behind. This is not the case at all. They make a great many foolish mistakes. They made a very foolish mistake last week when they started nuclear testing. That is just one example of how foolish they can be. They make mistakes in southeast Asia just as they make mistakes everywhere else. We have made mistakes in southeast Asia also. However, the fact is that in Laos, while the situation last May was extremely serious from a military point of view when this convention first met in Geneva, today it is very much better. It is just possible that the three parties in Laos will be able to agree on a government. It may not be the kind of government the west wants; of course it will not be. However, it will probably be the kind of government that the Laotians want; and after all, that is the main test. I think we must look at these problems in these other countries, from that point of view.
I agree with that statement.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As to Prince Sihanouk, the hon. member for Essex East says, "Oh, when we get a government, it will be a pro-communist government and the whole thing is terrible; we are just going to lose out right down the line". Let us try to be a bit more optimistic

Supply-External Affairs than that. We are going to have to face tensions of this kind not for a day or for a week but perhaps for ten years, 15 years, or 20 years and I think we must be a little bit more optimistic in our approach.
The hon. member mentions Cambodia. I think the head of state there resigned only as prime minister. I think he is still head of state. I refer to Prince Sihanouk. He is a very good leader. He was largely responsible for the conference taking place at all in Geneva. He went there and made a very statesmanlike speech in opening the conference. If things really work out in Laos it will be at least partially as a result of the leadership he gave. We have a skeleton commission in Cambodia. I do not know that they are needed there but Prince Sihanouk has asked that they remain. They are a great help in keeping peace in that country and in preventing either the communists or the western side from interfering, and he wants the commission to remain. He is extremely friendly to Canada. We have made a splendid contribution in that country and we intend to leave our representatives there as long as that situation continues.
In Viet Nam the commissioners deal with both North Viet Nam and South Viet Nam. They go over and visit the communists every once in a while and they come back to Saigon. We have plenty of trouble with that commission. The Polish representative and the Canadian representative do not always agree. Sometimes the Indian representative agrees with us and sometimes he agrees with the Poles. There have been many awkward situations but we are getting along and South Viet Nam has not fallen. I think the government of South Viet Nam is probably stronger now than it was a year ago. We are hoping that gradually this position will be worked out. In North Viet Nam, and South Viet Nam, Canada again is making a great contribution. It so happens that our commissioner there is Mr. C. J. Woodsworth, the son of J. S. Woods-worth, the founder of the C.C.F. party and he has been doing an excellent job.
These posts in southeast Asia are very difficult ones for Canadians. A fairly large group in the Department of External Affairs and in the Department of National Defence have now had service there. I believe this is one of the areas of the world in which Canada can help a great deal. We are not doing this under the United Nations. These commissions are in there as a result of having been set up at the Geneva conference in 1954. However, regardless of the fact that they are not United Nations commissions they are doing a good job. I realize that most of the reports from the region are full of woe and sadness and to the

effect that everything is going to pieces. However, the world has not gone to pieces yet. It may do so next week but it has not done so yet. In the meantime, let us keep our chins up.

I am sure that we all admire the minister's optimism. I suppose that a foreign minister must have optimism. However, I think it is the duty of an opposition, in the face of an optimism that is thought not to be fully realistic, to point out the situation as one sees it. I am not suggesting that the government of Canada or the minister, by their diplomatic efforts alone, can correct the situation. Obviously no one has made that claim. I am simply saying that from my own analysis of the situation-and I have been in the terrain and know the personalities involved- I do not share the confidence which the minister has in the situation.
He will recall having complained in this House of Commons, and properly so, about the inadequate air equipment, and the like, of the commission for the prosecution of its assignment which was, among other things, to see that there was a cease fire. Even at this late date the minister has indicated to the committee that there is a continuation of this problem of inadequate equipment. That situation, of course, arises not because Canada or the minister wants it to be the case but because there is on the part of someone a lack of co-operation which makes the work of the commission ineffective. I think the minister gave the basis for the complaint that exists, namely that the Soviet union and others are not interested in seeing an effective operation by the commission. That, of course, in itself is a serious matter. What I am saying is this. While one must not overstate a case, it is the duty of an opposition to anticipate. In this particular area we are seeing an operation that is causing concern and it will continue to do so unless there is an improvement through future developments. As long as the parties are talking in Geneva I do not suppose much that will be fundamentally damaging will eventuate.
All I am saying is that the protracted discussions indicate the importance of Indochina in the continuous effort of communist penetration taking place. I am not saying that we are losing at every point. I am not saying that the Soviet union is gaining at every point. I am not saying that it has not its adversities, drawbacks and failures. Of course it has. But what I am saying is that in this particular area, one of the vital areas in Asia, we are confronted with a situation which is part of these

various crises which confront us from time to time. Now it is Berlin. Tomorrow it will be somewhere else. Some day I am sure this particular situation will be another one about which we shall be registering our complaint against a policy of increasing illegitimate spheres of influence on the part of those who wish to impose the communist way of life on the rest of the world. I am not blaming the minister. I am not blaming the government. These are situations that have causes beyond the power of any one government to resolve. However, I do not believe that the situation in Indo-China is one that warrants the optimism of the minister. The minister will recall that two years ago he told us in this House of Commons that great progress was being made in disarmament. He did almost everything he could in that field, of course. We all know that. However, no great progress is being made in disarmament. It is well that we should look realistically at the situation so that we are not fooled by policies which may lull us for the moment but which eventually only play into the hands of those who se purpose it is to cause us to be complacent.
I speak thus not by way of criticism of the minister or of the government but to point out what I believe the real assessment of this situation should be.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am very glad the hon.
member tried to prove his case by referring to the question of disarmament. The idea seems to have been circulated that I am down in the dumps in regard to disarmament and have given up hope. Nothing could be further from the truth. I think the actual fact today is that because of the increased tension over Berlin and because of these nuclear tests millions upon millions of people around the world have decided their lives are in danger particularly from radiation. I believe the results will be a much greater urgency to the bringing about of a disarmament agreement at the next session of the general assembly of the United Nations than there has ever been before. There is not much point in giving up because that will not help anyone. What we want to do is stop this nuclear arms race which is becoming steadily faster.
While the unaligned countries at Belgrade last week may not have gone all out in their criticism of the Soviet union for conducting nuclear tests, their judgment in so doing has been to a degree backed up by the fact that within a very few days the United States announced its intention to conduct a nuclear test.
I have here a resolution passed by the unaligned countries on disarmament which reads as follows:
90205-6-5174
Supply-External Affairs
The participants in the conference consider that disarmament is an imperative need and the most urgent task of mankind. A radical solution of this problem, which has become an urgent necessity in the present state of armaments, in the unanimous view of participating countries, can be achieved only by means of a general, complete and strictly and internationally controlled disarmament.
As I said the other day there is a new disarmament plan which I think is very important, and which may well make quite a difference to this whole situation. There will be an opportunity in New York within the next few weeks to mobilize world opinion against this nuclear arms race.
I do not wish to do any boasting here today but from the time of the second world war Canada has taken her full part in trying to bring about disarmament. Certainly during the last two years we have been in the forefront in taking action of this kind, and I believe there is a reasonable chance that there will be some success at the coming session of the general assembly. Certainly we will do the best we can to mobilize world opinion on this question.
It is very heartening to realize that we have the support of both opposition parties. I know there is not one member in this house on the government side, in the Liberal party or in the New Democratic party, who will not be behind us in this effort. I am not suggesting we will succeed. After all, Canada is not running the world yet, but we will do what we can. I hope there will not be a lot of Jeremiahs and crape hangers here in Ottawa, not only in the House of Commons but in the press gallery as well, continually ridiculing what we are trying to do. This issue may involve the whole future of civilization and it is much too serious a proposition to have doubting Thomases all over the place. For goodness sakes, let the duly elected leaders in Canada sitting here in the House of Commons realize that fact. If people outside wish to do a lot of calamity howling, let them do it, but here we must keep our chins up and do the best we can to meet this situation.
I have a report of a speech made by general of the army, Douglas MacArthur, in Manila early in July which gives me great encouragement. General MacArthur in my judgment was the outstanding military leader of the last war. First of all he defended the Philippines and then fought his way back and throughout gave wonderful leadership. There has probably never been a better general in the history of warfare. The following is his statement:
General MacArthur said the advances in military weaponry have destroyed the possibility of war

Supply-External Affairs being used as a means for settling international differences. He said that if global war could be outlawed "it would mark the greatest advance of civilization since the sermon on the mount".
If there is one thing the peoples of the east and west share, it is a desire for peace, he continued. But, he added, the constant acceleration of the preparations for war may, without specific intent, precipitate "a cataclysm of destruction".
General MacArthur said the world's leaders "must have sufficient imagination and courage to translate the universal wish for peace".
That is the aim of the Canadian government.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think anyone would wish to underestimate the importance of the minister's determination and optimism in this matter of disarmament. While the difficulties seem to be greater than they were, I do not think any of us fully realize that as difficulties become greater, there is more incentive to greater action for their removal. There is no doubt about that in our minds. Of course we have to foe realistic as well, and the words used by General MacArthur, which have just been quoted-the fact that nuclear weapons have destroyed the possibility of war-merely meant they have destroyed the possibility of war in the minds of sane persons in the sense of war settled nothing. But the minister himself told us the other day that we were on the brink of nuclear war and destruction. That is why some of us feel a little depressed about the situation, as the minister no doubt does himself, not as a reason for sitting back and doing nothing, but as a reason for moving forward in an attempt to do more. I know the minister and our delegates will do what they can at the United Nations along these lines.
The specific item with which we are dealing has to do with Indo-China and control of the commission there in Laos. In this regard it is not easy to be optimistic about progress. The minister has referred to the difficulties of acquiring equipment to assure the function of the commission. I find it impossible to believe that this can be an insurmountable difficulty. If the will to make progress is there, there should not be much trouble finding equipment. Canada could itself supply the equipment which is required for this commission. The difficulty in respect to equipment, I am sure the minister will agree, has been manufactured or at least exaggerated by those who have other reasons for holding up progress in this matter. What worries us on this side, as I am sure it worries the government, is the possibility of these discussions in Geneva being used as a screen behind which the communists can build up their strength in Laos so that when the time comes to break
up the discussions it will be very hard to get them out of Indo-China and Laos. That is what worries us.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I pointed out to the hon. member for Essex East it was very difficult to get them out last May when the conference commenced. It cannot be harder to get them out than it was when we met in Geneva then, because the situation today is a great deal better than it was at that time.
This whole area may blow up. I cannot guarantee for a minute that it will not, but I think there is a reasonable chance that some settlement will be worked out.
We hope the minister is right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I should like to make a couple of remarks in connection with this vote for Canadian representation at international conferences, particularly in view of some of the comments that were made earlier today and in the past few years. I think it is necessary that our representatives at international conferences, particularly in their relations with the communists, understand one of the elements of the struggle which is going on.
I think it is quite obvious from what the hon. member from Kootenay West said today when he characterized the problem of Berlin as being a crisis over Berlin that apparently he does not appreciate what the real crisis is. It certainly is not over Berlin, it is over the struggle between the communists and the democratic world.
We have now the new leader of the New Democratic party, the premier of Saskatchewan, vacillating in his advice to the country. Two years ago he said we should be in NATO. A year ago he said we should be out of NATO. Now he says we should remain in NATO only as long as NATO does exactly what we say. This sort of advice betokens lack of understanding of the serious challenge which faces us from the communist forces.
There is one thought that I should like to place on record in regard to our general approach to the communist challenge. In the last few years great emphasis has been laid on the western responses to Soviet initiative. Often one hears that the west is losing the propaganda war, and assertions of a like nature, implying the conclusion that if we lose the propaganda war we will have lost to communism. I want to make it clear, Mr. Chairman, it is my view that no one can seriously contend that we are losing in the realm of ideas. Certainly, there has not been a single country in the world which had adopted communism by a free vote. There is not one government in the world which has had the misfortune to fall to the communists which has ever given its people the opportunity to vote itself out of communism. These are very well known facts but their significance to the communists is perhaps not as fully appreciated in the non-communist world. We sometimes think that by stating these facts the communists will feel abashed. In truth they do not feel abashed at all and the reason they do not feel abashed is to be found in the basic fundamentals of their creed. The communists basically do not hope to achieve their end by persuasion. They do not hope to achieve their end by argument. Communism, and this runs all
Supply-External Affairs through their creed, is based on force. Hon. members recall Lenin's statement on this subject:
Communism is the dictatorship of the proletariat, unrestricted by law, and based on force.
This has continued to be basic communist doctrine right down to the present time. The recent draft summary of the program of the communist party of the Soviet union which was sent to all members by the U.S.S.R. embassy in Canada restates the emphasis on force in several ways throughout its pages. I should like to draw attention to a statement on page three of this draft summary. It reads:
The practice of the world's greatest revolution and socialist transformation of society that has achieved unprecedented heights of development and advance, has confirmed the historic correctness of Leninism and dealt a smashing blow at the ideology of social reformism.
In other words, they say revolution is the means which has proved to be triumphant and it has dealt a smashing blow at reform, evolution, and that they say confirmed the correctness of the earlier statement of Lenin that I quoted.
Communism is based on force. It gains power by force. It maintains its power by force. This is an assertion with which most people will readily agree. The corollary of this does not find such ready agreement. The corollary is simply this, that propaganda, persuasion, though of importance in the communist armoury, is nevertheless of secondary importance in their thinking. They use force when they can get away with it. They use threats of force when they think that force itself is too risky and they use propaganda in between times, sort of like the ball players of a ball club talking it up until they get the ball again.
I submit there is importance in recognizing that propaganda to the communists is secondary and is not used chiefly for the purpose of proselytizing but rather as an adjunct to force, that propaganda with them is secondary to force, secondary to threats. Threats of force in undermining the will to resist of anybody who opposes them may not seem significant, but I think it is, and it probably explains Hungary and the recent nuclear explosions in Russia. The Prime Minister described those latter explosions as being contemptuous of world opinion and that statement could have been made about the earlier use of force in Hungary. In fact, as the communists' opportunities for gaining adherents diminish in the world, as they will in the western world and elsewhere where living standards are rising very rapidly, they will be able to rely less and less on propaganda. The old rallying cry of the communists used

Supply-External Affairs to be: "Workers of the world unite; you have nothing to lose but your chains". Obviously this cannot be so these days. This is the very point where the communists have failed most miserably, in helping the common man. It is the workers they have failed chiefly above everybody else. Here in the second decade of the second half of the twentieth century the standard of living of the Russian people, for example, and the others are even worse, is far behind ours, behind that of the United States and of western Europe even though they have greater natural resources, more people and more land than Canada and the United States.
I should like to remind the committee that there was something in Russia before 1917 and that other nations have rebuilt since 1917 to a far higher standard of living than the Russians have. The communists have failed to help the ordinary people. I think this is emphasized dramatically when one realizes that a person on unemployment insurance payments in this country gets more than the majority of working Russians-a person in receipt of social aid gets more than employed Russians.
Not only have the communists not been able to feed and clothe their people by twentieth century standards but in addition they have not given them freedom either. I suppose you could imagine somebody throwing back their phrase to them and saying, "Communists of the world join in free enterprise; you have nothing to lose but your chains". They would have a better opportunity to do so, of course, if they could get out of their countries, but the point I want to emphasize is that they have failed most significantly in the very areas of human endeavour where success would have helped them to persuade. They have deliberately concentrated their efforts in fact in those areas of human endeavour which help them to intimidate, threaten, bully and enforce by force communist rule. They have in fact placed guns before butter, fear before food and force before freedom. These things are of the essence when you consider dealing or treating with them, when we send our representatives abroad in order to meet the communists at international gatherings and when we try to lead them along the path of reasonableness.
I was much impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Greenwood the other day when he said that if we stick to it long enough perhaps they will lose their stimulus to aggression. We must stick to it in the meantime and never forget that at this time as in the past they rely chiefly on force. Therefore we must remain strong while we shift our response to their propaganda from the day-to-day meeting of their propaganda

utterances to an exposition of communism and an assertion of the positive values of the way of the western world in providing that happy combination of prosperity and freedom which it has been our good fortune to enjoy.
Mr. Chairman, does vote 83 cover all the international conferences to which we go during the year, including United Nations meetings? Does it cover all the expenses for Canadian representation?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

So the total rental we pay for accommodation at all our conferences during the year is $18,000. Is that correct? I am looking at page 181 where the details are given. They show that last year travelling expenses of Canadian representatives were $255,000. Presumably that included not only their travelling expenses but also their meals, accommodation and so on. Then there is a figure for rental of $18,000. Does that cover rental of all the space we use at all international conferences including the United Nations assembly, where I suspect we have to take a good deal of space in hotels?

speechtext: In the case of the delegation to the United Nations, for example, they would use the regular office of our permanent representative, and this rental of $18,000 apparently is only for odds and ends of accommodation. For example, in Geneva we have a villa for an office now. It is not half as good as it sounds. Various nations have villas in the suburbs. The grass is very long and there is a cow in the next field. But it does not cover hotel accommodation for delegates at meetings?

Mr. Chairman, this is a vote of $525,000 for the external aid office which is an increase of $70,000 over last year. Could the minister tell us something about the work of the office and whether it has succeeded in co-ordinating and bringing together all the activities of the government in so far as their administration is concerned in the field of international economic assistance?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
External aid formerly was divided among several departments, namely, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Finance and the Department of External Affairs. A committee of senior civil servants studied the situation and reported that it would be much more efficient to have one external aid office reporting directly to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. That was done last fall.
There was a great deal of work in setting up the office, but I am very pleased with the way in which it has been functioning. As the Leader of the Opposition knows, Mr. Moran is the director general of the external aid office. He came from a posting as high commissioner in Pakistan. I think there is excellent work being done.

I do know Mr. Moran and I think he is a very good man for this particular post. I know how efficient he is. I think it is an improvement over the previous situation to have the foreign aid co-ordinated in one office. This should make for efficiency and also for economy of administration.
Am I to take it that because of this development, which I think is a good one, all the recommendations to the government for foreign aid, the allocations for foreign aid, the responsibility in so far as officials are concerned for negotiations on those allocations, now go through this office to the minister and from the minister to the cabinet? It is all centralized in that way?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is an advisory board made up of the representatives of the three
Supply-External Affairs departments I have mentioned. Then, they make recommendations through the director general.

This would be a convenient item on which to say something about the principle involved in foreign aid. Canada has, of course, been a member of the Colombo plan from the very beginning. Since that time we have extended assistance to the West Indies, to certain countries in Africa under the special commonwealth African aid program, and we have likewise provided technical assistance under United Nations operations, and in other ways have given assistance to underdeveloped countries. There is a drive now under way, as the minister of course knows much better than I do, in the United States in particular, for increasing contributions on the part of nations that have been giving aid and nations that have not been giving assistance to underdeveloped countries. The President of the United States in his address in this house and in his inaugural speech, emphasized the growing awareness of the United States of the necessity for assisting underdeveloped countries on an increasing scale.
The United States government has, indeed, been seeking to persuade, and publicly, countries like West Germany and Japan to take a greater interest as donor countries in assistance to underdeveloped areas. I have recently been examining a publication prepared by Professors Millikan and Rostow, both of M.I.T., the latter now being one of the president's advisers, in which this whole problem is pointed up in an emphatic way. Their thesis is, of course, that in the light of the gross national product of certain countries, not enough assistance has been given by such countries to underdeveloped areas. The minister undoubtedly knows this publication. If he does not know it, he certainly knows the kind of thinking that now prevails in certain quarters, particularly in the United States.
Included among the countries regarded as not playing their full role is Canada. Canada is listed, I think, even below West Germany among those countries that did not give of their gross national product in proportion to other countries. This idea is going to receive increasing attention. It seems to me that it would be helpful if we could have from the minister some indication of the government's thinking in this particular. I am not seeking to be critical of the government because this program had its genesis under another administration. Looking at this problem objectively, I think one would want to know what recent thinking has meant. Are we going to make a real attack on poverty outside our

Supply-External Affairs own borders as well as at home. There has to be an increasing realization by countries who have been assisting underdeveloped areas of the need for an increase in the amount of their contributions.
The hon. member for Greenwood, of course, in the speeches he has made in this house has given us a lead, although he has not particularized the extent of the assistance we should provide in anything like the way Professors Millikan and Rostow have. We are all familiar of course, and the hon. member has helped familiarize us with the thinking and writing in this regard of Miss Barbara Ward who feels that the technique used in giving assistance under UNRRA might be used. In this way the total amount of foreign aid that is practical could be reached. Now, we are far short of her total figure. I am not now arguing for any particular figure for Canada, but it does seem to me, in the light of the thinking that is now going on particularly in the United States, we will not be able to escape a careful re-examination of the problem of foreign aid.
