AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to finish the train of thought I had just before the adjournment. I had just concluded indicating what appeared to be the attitude being taken, particularly in the United States, with regard to increasing, perhaps on a more rationalized basis, the assistance now accorded by well-known donor countries to underdeveloped areas.
I had said that in recent publications which obviously support the administration in the United States it has been suggested that certain countries, in relation to their gross national product, were not bearing a proportional responsibility for assistance to needy countries.
I do not believe, given all the facts and having in mind the various headings under which assistance is given both here and in other countries, Canada need feel it has shirked its responsibility. But I believe this matter is going to compel itself more and more upon us, as well as on other nations. We all recognize that in the interdependent world in which we live one of the instruments by which peace will be maintained, short of aggressive intentions and acts, will be by recognizing that other countries have to be given an opportunity to enjoy a higher

standard of life through improved literacy, stimulus of the productive processes of their economic systems, and the like.
It is not without significance that one finds, apart from governments, writers, students and zealous individuals reminding us that in this kind of world we are indeed our brother's keeper and that only by recognizing this fact will we be able fully to contribute to the existence of peace in the world.
The crash program offered to Latin America by the President of the United States, for instance, is only one example of the new thinking, the shift in emphasis and the leadership that is being provided. I mentioned declarations made by various leaders in different areas. I single one out, not because he is the only one to have done so but because his pronouncement was the last one of great significance. I refer of course to the recent declaration of Pope John XXIII in his encyclical, in which he reminded not only his own adherents but the people of the world of our common responsibility to help other countries.
This is a problem which is not as easy of solution as many people suggest, because we have problems at home, as have other countries. We have unemployment; we have other problems of a domestic character that demand attention. It is not easy for governments, in the face of such difficulties, to discharge what I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs of Canada recognizes as an essential direction that Canada must pursue.
It is true that we paid special attention recently to the request that came from the Prime Minister of India with regard to an accelerated form of assistance to the third five-year plan of India. In that connection we recall that Miss Barbara Ward, who has written so knowingly and brilliantly on these matters, has suggested that in the interests of world peace priority should be given by the donor nations to assisting India in the herculean task that lies ahead in the prosecution of her third five-year plan.
Canada has joined with the United States, and I believe the United Kingdom and France, in providing further assistance to India in this regard. That of course was a step which we commended in this house. I know, in the examination of this problem, that particularly in the United States, again, considerable attention is being paid to the methods employed in the administration of the funds being provided for needy countries.
Professor Galbraith, now the United States ambassador in Delhi, recently wrote a useful memorandum which I think is made public in the Foreign Affairs magazine. He outlined that there was not only a need for recognizing the increasing magnitude of this problem

and the responsibility thereby imposed on countries like Canada, Great Britain, France, West Germany, Japan and others, but it was also necessary to realize that while these funds would be necessary on an increasing scale to assist underdeveloped areas, some tighter form of administration should be employed to make sure the best use was being made of the assistance given. He lists priorities of regions of the world or of countries in those regions. For instance, he mentions that much money could be wasted by ignoring the lack of certain factors in certain countries that require assistance. I am sure the minister has borne in mind all of these things. He is undoubtedly much more fully aware of them than I am. However, I mention them because I believe we are now entering a new era of assistance to underdeveloped countries.
Over the week end I noticed that the President of the United States is about to invite, so it is said, a prominent and able financier in the United States to take charge of a program of foreign aid assistance of that country, based on recommendations which have been made by Mr. Labouisse who has done so much in the United Nations when on loan from the United States state department, and now serving his country in Washington. The plans envisaged, according to the report, flow from his recommendations. They support the thinking that I detect in suggestions made by Professor Galbraith and others. In any event I am sure the minister will be the first to recognize the importance of this kind of effort in confronting the terrible situation that faces mankind at the present time. Altogether apart from the exigencies and the dictates of their own foreign policies, the western countries partic-ulary, through the Colombo plan, have shown an objective interest in assisting other countries. We have been an original member of the Colombo plan organization for some time but, as I see it, we are now entering a new area of legitimate pressure to take an added load of responsibility. I am sure that the government is giving this matter careful consideration.
In making the remarks I have made today on this subject I have not had in mind any basis for criticism. I realize only too well the difficulties involved. However, it would be reassuring to know from the minister at first hand in this House of Commons, what the government's views regarding these matters are, as I think large sections of our people are interested in this problem. Does it share the general view taken by the present administration in the United States? Does it share the view that an examination should be made of the extent of contributions made by various countries as stated in the publications I have
Supply-External Affairs mentioned? What is the expectancy of trying to meet these further suggested contributions that are being proposed by so many private individuals like Miss Barbara Ward and more particularly by those in office today in countries that have been providing this assistance to underdeveloped areas? This is a problem that I know is not easy of solution. However, it is one we face and one from which we cannot shrink; and I am sure it is one that, over the years, will indicate the appreciation we have had of the nature of the problem which faces mankind at the present time.

I should like to raise on this particular item a few points having to do with the external aid office. Some of what I have to say will be in part repetition of matters I raised during the deliberations of the external affairs committee. However, before I begin, I cannot resist saying that I am waiting with fascination, after this afternoon's discussion, to find out whether the hon. member for Essex East has decided whether he is an optimistic pessimist or a pessimistic optimist. I hope he will let us know what his choice is in this regard before the conclusion of the discussion this evening.
I should also like to say that I congratulate the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the type of leadership they have provided in this whole debate and in this whole period of crisis and international tension that is upon us. It is refreshing to find a clear and concise statement of policy being made and being heard and understood by the people of Canada.
Having said that, one can hardly avoid mentioning the hon. member for Greenwood when one is discussing external aid. The service the honourable and distinguished gentleman has rendered to this house in the last few years in espousing the cause of the effectiveness and in fact the necessity of aid to the underdeveloped and uncommitted countries of the world cannot be overestimated or too highly praised. However, in these last few years-and I feel I am getting to be a bit of a bore on this subject-I have been trying without too much success-and I must add quickly "with some success"-to extract from the Department of External Affairs and in particular from the external aid office some visual representation of the program upon which Canada has embarked and proposes to embark in the future, something which can be taken by those of us who served on the committee and those of us in the house who are interested in this phase of external affairs and by means of which we can-and I suppose I am obliged to use the word-sell this program, this idea, the urgency of this type

Supply-External Affairs of thinking and the type of foreign aid program we have, not only to our constituents but to the people of Canada at large. There are many of us on the committee and there are other members in the House of Commons who are willing and anxious to do this missionary work. The minister has done a tremendous amount, as has the Prime Minister, the hon. member for Greenwood and others, in carrying this message in a general sense to the people of Canada. However, there are those of us who are willing and anxious to help in this work and we are most anxious to get the material which we can take to interested groups in our constituencies. I shall have something more to say later about the type of material I have in mind. It would be helpful if this program could be accelerated and this material could be placed in our hands with as little delay as possible.
During the discussions on the foreign aid vote in the committee on external affairs the witnesses before the committee, and Mr. Moran in particular, underlined the difficulties and the complexities that confront any government, particularly one in the northern hemisphere, in providing the type of aid needed in the form in which it is required by the recipient countries. There are difficulties of having available here the type of expert required with the type of expert knowledge which has the highest priority in the system of needs established by the nation requesting this assistance. This provides not only a challenge to the foreign aid office itself but to our universities and in a larger sense to our business and industrial communities. The type of expert assistance required in many foreign aid areas can only be given by those expert individuals urgently required by industry and business in general in this country. I suggest this situation provides a further challenge to the industrial community of this country.
These industrial communities are now faced with competitive price and production challenges and are responding to urgent government requests to meet the increasing competition for our traditional markets. We have already seen evidence that there is progress in this regard. However, the challenge must not only be to serve our national interest but to relinquish from time to time these skilled individuals in order that they may move to those underdeveloped countries to perform the tasks which must be accomplished there. From my personal experience in dealing with many individuals in this country there is an expressed desire to participate in this aid field. As was indicated during the committee hearing, many individuals have the desire but not the skill or, on the contrary, have the skill without the desire.

I suggest there are two facets involved in the solution to this problem. The first lies in the need of a long range program of the type we have heard announced in the United States by President Kennedy, encompassing a five year term of foreign aid. This program has been successful to a certain degree and is certainly a long range plan which will not be terminated after two or three years before its effectiveness has been accomplished.
The problem with which we are faced regarding this aspect of our program has reference to the expert assistance most required by recipient countries, which for several reasons is not available for one, two or more years. I feel that in addition to the sense of urgency which exists among the personnel of the department there should be a sense of urgency in respect to co-operation by other departments of government.
The public accounts committee discussed the Canada council scholarship program. That is something which will be under way over a fairly long period of time. However, there is a choice with respect to sending experts abroad to recipient countries or bringing individuals from those countries to Canada for training. I will have more to say regarding the problems involved here, but this is a challenge we must meet.
The Canada council has through its scholarship program offered great assistance to many individuals in the field of culture, But there is one individual studying fourteenth century wills in England. While this may be a tremendous advantage in the way of cultural development I suggest there must be a system of priority and emergency regarding the designation of the types of fields to be undertaken. Certainly in this world of today, faced with the compelling challenge of communism, the emphasis should be switched from the study and interest in fourteenth century wills to engineering, tropical agriculture and other faculties which lend themselves to humanitarian aid to the underdeveloped countries which is, after all, a long range challenge to democracy. There should be co-operation in government activities to assist in the training of individuals in logical and effective skills in order to help in the development of these countries.
Regarding the method of communication of this message to Canadians at large on as extensive a basis as possible, it is my understanding there are five thousand students from Asia, from Africa and the West Indies studying under one auspices or another in Canada, and who upon their graduation return to their respective countries. I suggest this is one area which represents a real challenge to Canada.

It has been stated today and on previous occasions during this debate that the west always responds to the activities of the communists-the communists act and we react, having lost our initiative. I suggest in a sense it could be argued that we have lost our initiative in the same way a dog has lost initiative until the flea bites him. However, I feel the problem is more profound than that.
It seems to me in this area a unique opportunity is provided for Canadians particularly around university cities. As I have indicated, there are approximately five thousand young men and women coming to Canada from Africa, from Asia and the West Indies and other similar areas. It is the flavour of democracy which they acquire during their experience here which will be of greater value to Canada and certainly to the cause of democracy generally than perhaps many of the millions of dollars spent in other ways, of which we will hear more later this week.
These young men and women will return to the countries of their origin and will become beyond any shadow of a doubt the leaders and members of the corps surrounding the leaders which will guide their respective nations to their ultimate destinies in the coming generation.
This surely represents a challenge to Canadians which I am sure has already to some degree been accepted by groups who are actively sponsoring students in this country. The universities as well as other nonuniversity organizations have done a great deal in this field through providing facilities by which those individuals can meet with Canadian students. I feel that much more can be done in this direction by inviting these students from the universities into our homes and communities in order that they may see something of democratic society rather than strictly classroom activity in Canada.
I am proud to say that when this question was raised in the external affairs committee an important statement was made regarding the necessity for co-operation and assistance of the Canadian public at large, and that when I returned to my constituency, having contacted six or seven organizations and outlined the magnitude of the problem, I discovered each and every one of these organizations either undertook to bring the problem to the attention of their executives or, as my own service club indicated, something is being done in this regard at this present time. I feel this is of tremendous advantage in showing these foreign students something of the fibre and character of our democratic society.
As I suggest, this is being carried on by university women's groups, women's auxiliary groups, church groups, service clubs and
Supply-External Affairs others. I am convinced there are many others who would co-operate and continue to do so in the same way after being convinced of the necessity and importance of this type of progress.
As I have said earlier, this field represents a challenge we as Canadians certainly can accept. By continuing the good work in this direction, already to no little extent commenced, we can provide the bulwark of education in democracy and counteract the propaganda on the part of the communists. The flavour that these young people take home with them will not only represent the flavour of Canada but that of democracy as well. It is unfortunate that in certain cases we have failed in the past. I hope by offering an example without naming the particular location it will help to underline the problem without incurring any criticism.
It is a fact in recent years a girl student from Pakistan spent three full academic years winter and summer in one of our major Canadian cities. At no time in that three years had she been invited inside a Canadian home. I leave it to the hon. members to ask themselves this question: had they been in a similar situation and studying in a foreign land what would be their opinion after three years of that kind of treatment?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am sure hon. members will have taken careful note of the remarks of the Associate Minister of National Defence and one of the members for Queens, Prince Edward Island, on the first item of these departmental estimates, which derived in part from their recent attendance as observers at the meeting of the inter-American economic and social council at Punta del Este. What I have to say on this item is to be very brief and is intended in no way to be competitive with the suggestions they made with respect to the deepening and broadening of Canadian contacts with Latin America. However, I did feel that the want of some reference in the debate on the estimates to another area in which Canada has had deep and abiding connections might all unintentionally be taken as an indication of lesser concern among Canadian members of parliament. I refer to the West Indies.
During the past few years Canadian aid to the West Indies has operated under a program of assistance which was set up to cover the period from April 1, 1958 to March 31, 1963. The sum of $10 million was allocated by the government for expenditure during this period. A major part of this money, about $6 million was spent on two ships requested by the West Indies for interisland trade, the Federal Maple and the Federal Palm. The Federal Maple is now in service
8196	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs in the West Indies. I had the pleasure of seeing her arrival in Port-of-Spain less than a month ago. Other projects under the Canadian aid program include the spending of a million dollars on the construction of a dock in St. Vincent. Equipment for harbour facilities is being provided for several of the smaller territories. As Canadians we shall also be carrying out a natural resources survey in Dominica and we shall be providing some $50,000 worth of equipment for a technical school in the lovely island of St. Christopher.
In the area of technical assistance a wide variety of experts from Canada has been sent to the West Indies. Their interests have covered a very wide range, from banking to teaching, and from postal service to public works, particularly in the field of housing. On the other hand, trainees have been sent to Canada for experience in public administration, in fisheries and in other fields of public endeavour. These are all in addition to the students qualifying for scholarships under the commonwealth scheme.
At the present time a joint survey is in progress in which Canada is participating with the United Kingdom and the United States to ascertain further needs of the smaller territories of the West Indies which have now set May 31, 1962 as the target date for their independence and their achievement of dominion status.
We in Canada intend to use a substantial portion of this aid program of $10 million, about $1J million of it, in assistance to the smaller territorial islands which compose the West Indies. The University College of the West Indies has been promised assistance. This will take the form of a residence for engineering students.
May I make this earnest suggestion to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who has the highest regard for and interest in the welfare of the West Indies as he has in other areas and urge him to take into consideration the possibilty of a further program of Canadian helpfulness to the West Indies within the concept of commonwealth brotherhood.
Speaking as a private member, may I say I do not personally favour a fixed term or a fixed amount. I suggest that probably it is not within the Canadian tradition to travel about the world with a satchel full of money. Probably it is not within our competence and it is not our style. I think a better program would be one in which we would give a firm and clear assurance to the West Indies that, in the interest of our historic connection, of our common bond of government philosophy, government practices, government ideas and ideals, within the framework of our commonwealth brotherhood, we will not hesitate


to bring before parliament measures originating in the West Indies, suggestions created in their own area, on which they desire our further assistance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, Canada's record in the field of external aid has been excellent from the start and in my judgment it continues to be properly described by that adjective. Mind you, in some ways we are an underdeveloped country. There is quite a difference between the capacity of Canada and that of some of the older countries, such as the United States, West Germany and the United Kingdom, to provide aid of this kind.
I was a little surprised to hear that some United States writers had been pointing the finger at Canada and had been saying that she should contribute more. That is not a very effective way of getting results. I would point out that I think that the Canadian aid has been quite a lot more effective in gaining friends for Canada abroad than has been the case with aid from some of the other nations which are now being a little critical of us.
We have been spending a great many million dollars each year for aid and I think that those payments have been supported by Canadians from coast to coast. Since I have been minister in this department I have heard very few complaints about Canada supplying aid.
Naturally we would like to get more money for the external aid office. The more money we can get, the better, because it makes our position much easier. We are able to make bigger fellows of ourselves and win more friends for Canada. But you know where the money comes from and we can only get so much.
Hon. members might be surprised to hear of the different ways in which we give aid. For example, under the Colombo plan there is an amount of $50 million a year, which is $15 million more than the former government gave-
There has been some inflation since.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-for aid to Burma, Ceylon, India, Indonesia, Malaya, Pakistan, Viet Nam, Cambodia, Laos and indirectly to Thailand under the Mekong river project, and in addition there is technical assistance under that plan. Then there are the Canada-West Indies aid program, the special commonwealth African aid program, the commonwealth technical assistance scheme, the commonwealth scholarship and fellowship plan in which Canada is providing one quarter of the thousand scholarships which are given throughout the commonwealth, the United Nations expanded program of technical assistance to underdeveloped countries, the

United Nations special fund, the United Nations technical assistance training centre at the University of British Columbia, the Indus basin development fund, the international development association, the international bank, the international finance corporation, the general fund of the international atomic energy agency, the Manitoba technical assistance scheme, which is a new scheme in which the federal government and the government of Manitoba are co-operating, and educational assistance to French speaking Africa. That is quite a list of schemes under which Canada is providing aid.
We try to provide this aid in an efficient way. There is not a great lot of ballyhoo about it and no great publicity campaigns but I suggest to members of the committee that it is very effective and that Canada has no reason whatsoever to feel ashamed of the effort she is making in this worthy field. We will do our utmost as time goes on. There is no question of the government's not being anxious to help in these different fields. For example, we are now giving consideration to a type of Colombo plan in the Caribbean area. This would include not only the West Indies Federation but, probably, British Guiana and British Honduras. I do not know whether we can work that out but we would like to initiate some plan of that type.
It is very helpful to have the submissions made by hon. members in the house. These always have some influence with the finance department, and I am very grateful for the suggestions that have been made by members who have taken part in the discussion of this item.

Mr. Chairman, I have already exposed the house to two or three speeches on this question and I shall not weary hon. members tonight. I shall be very brief but I did not want to miss the opportunity to put in my oar, however briefly.
I was happy to hear the recital by the minister of the things we are doing and which we know are worth while. I do not need to be told that the government is sympathetic. It is fair for us to remind the committee of the addition made to the Colombo plan and it is also proper for us to remind ourselves that the Secretary of State for External Affairs sometimes needs assistance in getting the moneys he would like from some other ministers whom we know and respect and whose duty it is to act as watchdogs. Accordingly I want to put on the record two or three things which have been said before, which are obvious but true, which are compelling and which if we disregard I believe we shall rue the day.
Supply-External Affairs
There are, of course, three obvious arguments which we have heard again and again for aid to underdeveloped countries. For the moment I am thinking about the east, India and the other countries of that area. First of all, there is the humanitarian argument. If these people were going to bed hungry just across the road from us we would not go to bed until we had done something about it. Second, there is the political argument which is that it is tremendously in our interests, indeed, it is vital to us, that these underdeveloped countries shall develop economically under free institutions and not under communist institutions. What we would feel like if we heard tomorrow morning that India had decided to proceed from now on under communist institutions I do not like to think. Then there is the third argument, the economic argument, which some people rather deprecate because it sounds as if we were doing it for our own interests. I have no objection to doing something in our own interests as long as it is in the interests of other people too.
I want to give two illustrations to show what can happen as a result of foreign aid. They have both been given in the house before. One is the case of a project under the Colombo plan to which we contributed $37 million. It is worth saying again and again, for the benefit of those people who think that such sums represent barrels of dollars shipped abroad, that of that $37 million 95 per cent was represented by Canadian employment. In other words, 95 per cent of what we sent was Canadian goods or services.
The other thing I should like to reiterate and which I do not think can be said too often has to do with what happened in 1946 when we lent $1J billion to Britain. At that time the then minister of finance used as his strongest argument the point that we were going to finance people who would make purchases from us. This they did in a big way. A very large percentage of that $1J billion was used to buy goods in Canada.
I have one other thing I want to say. When the matter of aid is brought up I often find people saying that the money is misused, that there is corruption and lack of wisdom, and that really what we should be doing is simply sending out teachers and so on. That of course should be done. I welcome what the hon. member for York-Scarborough said tonight. It was really heartening to hear what he had to say about the way his projects were taken up. I just want to make the point that we here can do so much to help ourselves as well as others by this project, by sticking to it, by
8198	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-External Affairs feeling that it is part of our job and by feeling that unless we go through with it not only the other people concerned but we ourselves are going to suffer.

Mr. Chairman, this vote gives us the opportunity to discuss the general question of external aid. Perhaps by spending some time on it we may save time on the details of international economic assistance which are included in the following votes. I must say that I have some sympathy with the minister in his desire to discharge his obligations and the obligations of Canada in respect of international economic assistance. I know that he will get more trouble from the Department of Finance and the Minister of Finance than he will from the opposition in this regard because, however idealistic a view we take about our obligations in this matter and what we ought to do, we come up against the exigencies of domestic affairs and the desire of the Minister of Finance to balance his budget. As a result, these considerations of domestic policies, and this does not apply to any particular government at any particular time, perhaps have an effect on what we can do in the field of international economic assistance. There is always a relationship between what can be done in Canada for people who need help and what can be done for people in Pakistan who need help.
But the fact remains, Mr. Chairman, that in world opinion we are considered, and indeed we are, a fortunate, developed and rich country with a very high standard of living. We are expected, therefore, to play our part in bringing about a situation in the world where we will not have rich countries and slum countries, developed countries and underdeveloped countries. I do not know whether or not the minister agrees with me, but I have found that the use of this word "underdeveloped" in respect of countries that we are trying to assist economically can lead to serious trouble. Some of these countries that are now economically poor in relation to ours are far more developed in some other ways than we are. Some of these countries we are privileged to assist in the field of industrial development now had civilization long before we were even in North America.
When we talk about underdeveloped countries, therefore, we are thinking only of material underdevelopment. The fact remains, and I think statistics will show this, that in spite of the assistance which the richer countries have been able to give to some of the poorer, the gap between the richer and poorer countries rather than being remedied or lessened in the last 10 or 15 years, has perhaps increased. This is a sad commentary on planetary development. We still have, therefore, in

our own country an obligation, along with other countries, to do what we can to change this process and to lessen that gap.
I have recently, Mr. Chairman, been attending a private and unofficial meeting at Oxford university on the subject of tensions which arise out of development. At this conference the majority of the members were from Asia and Africa, from what we call the materially underdeveloped countries. I found it extremely interesting to listen to them talk about their economic, their development problems and the tensions that arise out of these problems. They feel that we in the western world, in what they consider to be the more developed and more fortunate countries from an industrial and economic point of view, can do much to help them sort of leap out of their situation into one which I suppose it has taken the western countries a thousand years to develop. They want to do it in a few years, to leap out of a subsistence economy into an economy which will provide them with television sets and what they consider to be the advantages of a material civilization. They are going to try to do that in 25 or 30 years, and it has taken other countries 600 or 1,000 years to do it.
They are not going to be content with the slow progress of industrial development we have had to face in the western world over these generations. They do feel, whether or not they are right, that we owe them something in this regard because most of them were colonial countries. They have a feeling that what they call the imperialist colonial countries of the west, somehow or other held them up and if it had not been for colonial occupation they might have made more progress. I think that is a very dubious doctrine, myself, but that is the way they feel. They expect this help from us, therefore.
I got the impression, not only at this meeting but at other meetings I have had- the minister I think must have acquired the same impression-that the value of the kind of assistance we are giving them in these estimates, and for the year 1961-62 we are providing $61,122,445 of help, is not to be determined by the number of dollars we are making available but by the spirit and understanding we show in relation to their problems. I think Canada has achieved a very good reputation in this regard, not merely because of or primarily because we have been able to help them through this appropriation, but because we have shown in Asia and in Africa, an understanding of their problems and sympathy for their difficulties. You cannot estimate the value of this in dollars and cents. We give them this help, not charity. They are very sensitive about that. If we give them the feeling we are

Supply-External Affairs
doing something to help them, we do not get very far. It is not a matter of charity at all. They are very suspicious, and I am sure the minister knows about this, about help that is given to them in terms of the effect it will have on their association with us in the cold war.
We have made a good deal of progress in this regard, I think, in the last five or ten years, as I think the United States has. Economic assistance of this kind, if it is related to the cold war, is not going to do any good at all. The United States has had some rather disillusioning experiences. They have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into a country, and at the end of that time have found themselves more unpopular than before they gave anything at all. I think we have learned from that. I do not believe we can keep cold war considerations entirely out of economic assistance. I do not believe we could be expected, in Canada any more than in any other country, to give assistance to countries if that assistance is likely to be used against us politically. However, we cannot expect to get any results from economic assistance which is given to countries because we hope that by giving that assistance they will line up with us in the cold war. I think we have made a good deal of progress in the last few years in that regard. We help these countries because it is a good thing for us to do, it is a good thing for the peace of the world and because the world is one. Indeed, the world cannot exist half poverty stricken and half an affluent society.
In these discussions we have had during last week and which we have had previously, and the minister has attended a good many of them, there has been a good deal of argument as to how this assistance can best be given. Some of the items that follow this item deal with bilateral economic assistance and some of them deal with multilateral economic assistance. The general impression I got from talking to the representatives of what we call the receiving countries is that they would like to get their assistance on a multilateral basis so that there will be no suspicion of political strings attached. This is the reason we should undertake, whenever we can, to channel assistance through multilateral agencies, not by direct bilateral deals. I think, as realistic people, we must understand that while that is the ideal there is no possibility of the United States, for instance, and the United States is the greatest source of assistance in this field, channelling most of its aid multilaterally or through the United Nations. I think we have to accept that fact, that in a good many situations the most effective, the most practical way of doing it now is
by government to government. In that kind of operation, we can only hope that there will be a minimum of political strings attached.
I think, as I have said, we have made a good deal of improvement on that account in the western world in recent years. I recall arguing, at this particular meeting, with one of the African delegates on this question of strings attached. Unfortunately, most of these representatives of new countries recently emerged from colonial status are unduly sensitive about this question. They are almost morbid in their sensitivity about this. Every time they accept something they have the feeling that perhaps there is a string attached to it. However, it is not difficult to point out to them that if you get any kind of help from anybody in any situation, there are strings attached. If you have a private loan from a bank there is a string attached. We who are contributing countries should do what we can to make as certain as possible that the aid we give will be used for constructive purposes. We do this in the Colombo plan because there are strings attached to our aid under that plan. But they are only that the money we give will be constructively used. Because we discuss this with the receiving countries there is no feeling of suspicion attached to that particular string.
As one of the African delegates said to me a couple of weeks ago, "It is bad enough to have aid with political strings attached, but it is much worse to have political strings without any aid." Perhaps that is true, but I think we have got through that stage now. We used this approach continually in our discussions. I cannot think of any better way of providing assistance, apart from the United Nations, which is the ideal way of doing it than through such schemes as the Colombo plan. But there are limitations of practicability which we have to accept as realistic people to multilateral help. However, apart from the United Nations the best way of giving this help is through projects, procedures and mechanisms such as we have worked out under the Colombo plan arrangements. There we have a kind of multilateral arrangement with bilateral conversations between the receiving and distributing countries.
We had a great deal of discussion about this in Oxford a couple of weeks ago. I do not think the Colombo plan countries who have received aid from the contributing countries have ever felt at any time there was any string attached to that aid which was not justifiable. I think that is the way it should be done.
Reference has been made to the fact that we are not doing as much in Canada as we should. Perhaps no country at the present
8200	HOUSE OF
Supply-External Affairs time is doing as much as it should. At this particular meeting in Oxford we did not pass any resolution but there was a feeling that every contributing country should give one per cent of its national income for international economic assistance. If we relate our contribution of $62 million to our national income we are well below that 1 per cent. I think that is a desirable objective toward which we should work. I do not know whether my hon. friend from Essex East will agree with me on this, but I am not too much impressed with the fact that we should have a level of 1 per cent right across the board. After all, we have the principle of graduation in income tax, and I think those who are the richest should accept greater obligations than those who are not quite as rich. But I have no doubt in the world that we can do more.
This is not a political matter because more is being done now than was done a few years ago. Our income has grown and so has our contribution to economic assistance. However I think we can still do a great deal more and I think we should do more, because after all $40 million, $50 million or $100 million which is wisely spent in international economic assistance in the right places at this time might do more to increase stability and security in the world than spending $100 million or $150 million on some forms of arms defence.
Therefore without criticizing the minister or the government in what has been done I express the hope-and I feel quite strongly about this-that perhaps we can do more in the future than we have in the past in making this contribution, not so much to assist other countries but to assist ourselves; to assist security and stability in the world. I wish the minister well in his conflict with the Minister of Finance in this field.

Mr. Chairman, I had intended to say a few words along the line just expressed by the leader of the official opposition. There is no necessity for me to take the time of the committee to repeat what he has said, except to say that we wholeheartedly support the remarks he has just made with respect to external aid and his suggestions with respect to our actions in the future.
I have just now returned from a reception given by the high commissioner for New Zealand. Strangely enough, I had an opportunity to talk with several representatives of countries interested in this type of aid from Canada. What the leader of the official opposition said is quite correct. I have heard it repeatedly. They very much appreciate our methods in this respect. They appreciate 

the fact that there are no strings attached and they are willing to co-operate with us to make certain the money is expended to their best advantage. I think our record throughout the world stands very well and in this respect I think the department has carried on the traditions of this country very well indeed.
I think it was a very good move to bring this type of assistance under the administration of one head, that is, external aid. I think it has brought together the loose ends and will make for even greater efficiency in the future. In conclusion I wish to say that, like the leader of the official opposition, we hope we can continue to do more and more in this respect. I say this because we believe this type of assistance and a program of co-operation builds good will within and without the commonwealth and is the sort of sound foundation to lay for the building of peace in the future.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 88 carry?

Mr. Chairman, there is one other matter I wish to raise before vote 88 carries. I referred to it last Thursday when speaking on the first item of the debate that began that day.
I mentioned then that when the Associate Minister of National Defence was attending the recent conference in Uruguay as an official observer from Canada he had declared publicly that there was a necessity for extending economic aid to Latin America. I am not now suggesting a program, but when a minister of the crown takes publicly a position, I think it is incumbent upon him or his colleagues to indicate if he reflected government policy.
I believe that what the minister said a moment ago about the extent of our assistance was right. I think Canada is performing very outstanding work in the field of assisting economically underdeveloped areas. I observe the admonition of the Leader of the Opposition who so correctly stated that he thought we perhaps misrepresented the situation when we simply referred to underdeveloped countries.
The Associate Minister of National Defence made some very important observations. He said, for instance, as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail on August 24, 1961:
-Latin Americans need help financially and technically to keep them from going communist.
He said, inter alia:
Their sympathies are with us now... We should keep it that way.
Then he said:
The feature that struck me was that Latin America seems to be at the crossroads. Either they will advance and achieve prosperity and progress through democratic free enterprise, or some nations

-unless they find a solution to their problems- quite easily will fall prey to communist theories and methods.
These are very important words. They would be important from the mouth of any public man, but when they issue forth from one who holds a position in the government of Canada I think they call for comment in this house. Was the associate minister indicating that the Canadian government has plans to join with the United States in its program of economic assistance? It may be that we have to look at those areas in the world where we can give assistance. There certainly is a limit to what countries can do. I have certainly not suggested that we have reached that limit; I have simply pointed out what the Associate Minister of National Defence said. In addition to the important matter of assistance to Latin America, it raises another matter that is not unrelated. I have suspected that one of the reasons why the government was not prepared to join the organization of American states, altogether apart from the initial contribution involved in such membership, was that there would inevitably flow from it some pressure to extend to Latin American countries a form of economic assistance that is non-existent now as far as Canada is concerned. When this matter was discussed in April the Prime Minister had indicated that when the departmental estimates were before the house, it would be given an opportunity of expressing its views. One drew the inference that the government at that time would indicate what its intentions were with regard to joining the organization of American states.
Twice in this house, namely last Thursday and last April, I have stated-and the Leader of the Opposition last April expressed his view as well

that the time had come when we should join the organization of American states. The mere joining of that organization does not in itself create any obligation on our part to extend economic aid to Latin American countries. That is something that we must consider in the light of our responsibilities toward these and other countries. However, it seems to me that some time before this item is passed the minister might find it convenient to indicate what the government's intentions are with regard to the kind of declaration made by his colleague the Associate Minister of National Defence and whether or not the government has reached a decision with regard to what might be regarded as a corollary problem, namely the proposal that we have obligations to countries in the sister American continents as well as to countries which are joined with us for defensive purposes in other organizations and with whom we are
Supply-External Affairs associated in the United Nations for the purpose of trying to mitigate the causes of war and to preserve world peace.
There is in this country a strong body of opinion that believes strongly that, because of our ties with Latin America culturally, in terms of language, religious community of interest and other common participations, we owe to them and to ourselves an affiliation such as that which would come from membership in the organization of American states. I would put it on a political ground, namely that the problems of our hemisphere are now giving evidence of increasing acuteness and possible danger that will affect us as well as the United States. We have a special point of view and a special interest which, notwithstanding the difficulties, it seems to me could be discharged more effectively by our accepting that responsibility. That responsibility in itself does not necessarily mean embarking at this time on programs that may be regarded as being beyond our financial capacity.
I simply make one further observation in this regard. Whatever reasons there were in the past for non-participation or for nonmembership, they do not seem to exist today. Commonwealth considerations or the attitude of the United States certainly are no longer valid reasons. Indeed we all recall the suggestion-and I am not now speaking of the propriety of it-made by the President of the United States in this House of Commons with regard to our membership. I am not saying that the President had no right to make that statement but I would have thought that, unless the matter had been cleared with the Canadian government beforehand, a more effective way of persuading us to join the organization would have been to refer to it possibly in talks privately with the minister over the tea table, if that is the kind of thing the minister has when he meets with a president around a table. In any event, I think this is an important matter and in view of the statement of the Prime Minister it would seem to me that there ought to be some declaration forthcoming from him.
Before this item passes may I ask the minister another question, namely whether the devaluation policy of the government in any way affects the real value of our aid to these countries.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Leeds is no, Mr. Chairman, because the bulk of the money is actually spent in Canada. The hon. member for Essex East rather surprises me because he has become such a great enthusiast for Canada joining the organization of American states.

Supply-External Affairs
Inspired by the leadership of the hon. gentleman a year ago.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He is the one convert I have made to this policy.
And the member from Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
For 22 years I sat over there on the opposition side and not any kind of move was made by the Liberal government. However, in the last couple of years they have begun to grow enthusiastic. Perhaps they are learning, after a quarter of a century.
During these last two years we have been moving to strengthen Canada's relations with all of the Latin American countries. I think this has been a very important policy. The hon. member for Essex East referred to the statement made by the Associate Minister of National Defence who led a Canadian delegation to the meeting of the inter-American economic and social council held in Uruguay last month. That council was called together in order to consider ways of promoting economic growth and social development in Latin America. Our delegation has come back with very helpful information about Latin American conditions and in addition has made further friendly ties with all of the countries of Latin America. Had there been a meeting of the organization of American states this year we would have been represented by an observer delegation. That meeting was to have been held in Quito in February but it has been postponed indefinitely. When it takes place, however, a Canadian delegation will be in attendance.
In addition to that, we have decided to apply for membership in the United Nations economic commission for Latin America. This commission was established in 1948 by the United Nations in order to assist in raising the level of economic activity in the Latin America area, to strengthen economic relations between the countries of the region and other countries of the world and to carry out technical assistance programs in that area. Besides the 20 republics of Latin America, its membership includes the United States, France, the United Kingdom and the Netherlands. The West Indies and British Guiana have become associate members and British Honduras has applied for the same status. Membership would provide a specialized forum in which to watch Latin American trade, policies and practices and a possible way to influence those countries away from protectionism and bilateralism, it will permit Canada to participate in the formation of policies for the area and possibly place us in a better position to supply capital goods to the mutual benefit of Latin American countries
and Canadian industry. It would also facilitate the search with other American nations in the appropriate bodies for solutions to the growing problem of raw material prices and production.
We have no plan under which we make bilateral contributions to Latin American countries. However, they do benefit under United Nations plans.
No record is kept of what proportion of Canada's contributions to those funds is used in Latin America but through that channel there is help given. There is also some help given in the way of scholarships by the Canada council and by the national research council. I would be very pleased in this field as well as in the general external aid field to be able to do a great deal more than we have been doing up to the present time. In my view there is another field in which help is being given and that is through the Export Credits Insurance Act. For example, arrangements have been made for guaranteeing payment for a big shipment to Chile. Some months ago there was a similar arrangement made for the export of steel rails to Mexico. Help of this kind is given and, incidentally, I think that kind of help should be included in the 1 per cent figure that the people in the United States talk so much about. They include everything they give in their 1 per cent figure and we can justifiably include guarantees of this type as well in that figure.
In so far as diplomatic representation is concerned, we have extended our diplomatic relations in Latin America. On Saturday I hope to sign an exchange of notes with the Guatemalan ambassador to the United States by which our ambassador in Mexico will be accredited to Guatemala. This will leave only one Latin American country with which Canada does not have diplomatic relations, namely, El Salvador. I think within a matter of months we can make a similar arrangement for representation in that country.
Another method by which contacts have been increased is by exchange of visits. Our own Prime Minister visited Mexico City, returning a visit by the President of Mexico. I have visited in Argentina, Chile and Peru. There has been also the recent visit of the Associate Minister of National Defence. On November 27 the president of Argentina is to come to Canada where he will pay a visit lasting three or four days.
I suggest we have moved very rapidly, certainly in comparison with any movements made by the Liberal government to strengthen ties with Latin America. In due course the curiosity of the hon. member for Essex East with regard to this question of joining the organization of American states will be

satisfied. However, I point out to him that one of the least effective ways of persuading Canada to adopt a policy is for the president or the head of state of another country to come here and tell us what we should do, no matter if it is done with the best intentions. Even when it is done in that way it is not the best way to get results, and I am rather surprised that the hon. member would suggest that we should at once have jumped through the hoop when the President of the United States made this suggestion.
He has not been in politics as long as you and I have.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I suggest that is going quite far in advocating policy, but I do not think President Kennedy meant to interfere.
However, I explained some months ago that we thought this was a policy in respect of which the Canadian people should have an opportunity to consider; to see what they thought of it. There is greatly increased interest in the whole question as a result of President Kennedy's speech. Perhaps it is in the wrong way, but certainly it is increased interest. I think today there is more interest being taken in this question in Canada than there has been in the last 25 years, and there is an opportunity being given for public opinion to build up and, after all, in some cases that is not a bad idea. Certainly we do not have to rush into new policies. This would represent a major change in Canadian foreign policy. I feel it will be of great value to have the Canadian people realize just what the implications of such a move would be.

Mr. Chairman, we are not asking the minister with a view to having the association jump through the hoop merely on the suggestion of the President of the United States that it would be a desirable jump. Nor are we asking him to rush into this. As a matter of fact, long before the President made the statement in this house, the minister's predecessor had us at least half way through the hoop three years ago. The minister is now saying that what we have to do is give the people of Canada a chance to think about this matter. We must find out how they feel about it, giving the Canadian Institute of International Affairs an opportunity to tell us what to do, and that in due course we will make up our minds. While we all grow, I hope, in wisdom and stature in this particular situation, the opposition's interest has I think increased, but the minister's has lessened. The minister used to have very definite views about OAS. I must say I was impressed by his arguments of those days in favour of a particular course and assumed that when he had the responsibility he would implement
Supply-External Affairs the particular advice he gave us then. I think there is a good deal to be said for closer association with the organization of American states. We have made our position very clear on that point.
The minister has pointed out there have been other forms of closer association with Latin America. That is quite true. Diplomatic representation of Canada in this part of the world has grown; as it was always intended that it should grow. In the years after world war II we opened embassies and legations in various parts of the world, and the Latin American states were always on the list. But it was always a question of priority and finding the money in the Department of Finance, as well as the people to man the new posts. It is a good thing that representation in Latin America has developed. I think we are all in favour of that development. It certainly is a good thing that the minister and, of course, the Prime Minister can go down to Latin America to cultivate close and friendly contacts with the leaders of those governments. But there is this question which is predominant now in the public mind regarding the actual association of Canada with this particular western hemisphere organization. In consideration of this in the past I admit some worry about membership which meant some responsibility in the development of the organization because we were joining a lot of international clubs at that time. I think there was a limit at that time to what we could or should do, but circumstances have changed. There is now the fact that we are so worried about the establishment of communist bases on the western hemisphere and the feeling we have that the United States should be careful before it reacts too rashly to such a development. If we are to give the United States this kind of advice, as we did and rightly during the Cuban mix-up, and if we are to interest ourselves in these developments, then I think we have to take our responsibility in the organization which is concerned with these matters namely the organization of American states.
In his recent visit to the conference in Uruguay-and reference has been made to that-I think the Associate Minister of National Defence performed two very useful services. According to the press he stopped a revolution in Argentina, and he also brought home to us the importance of doing what we can in the richer countries to assist the poorer countries in Latin America; otherwise there is going to be very serious trouble down there. I thought that perhaps, in the light of that particular report by the Associate Minister

Supply-External Affairs of National Defence, the minister and the government had made up their minds to take responsibility without waiting for the report from the Canadian Institute of International Affairs and would now associate Canada with the organization of American states.

I want to ask the minister this question arising out of his remarks. In referring to ways in which we had contributed aid in South America he included two items of assistance. I have one in particular in mind. He included as an item of assistance the insurance contract made under the Export Credits Insurance Corporation legislation. I am quite sure he did not intend that result to flow from his remarks. I have particular reference to the $12 million contract of assistance where capital goods were supplied to Chile. I think the minister will be very quick to agree with me that the purpose of that legislation was to enable our producers and manufacturers in Canada to compete more successfully with the producers in other countries that have the production capacity; and that from the point of view of the recipient country the benefit to them from our having this long term insurance or guarantee of the seller's contract is very little indeed because had they not got it from us they would presumably have got the capital equipment from another country. I would hope the minister would take a moment to correct any impression that may inadvertently have been created by his remarks that was not in accordance with the facts.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think this is done under section 21, of Part II of the act. In recent months this has been used in effect to help not only the Canadian firm but also the recipient country by giving extended credit which it could not get otherwise. In each of the cases I mentioned there was quite a large element of helping out the respective governments of Chile and Mexico. The same plan has been used with other countries, some of which are getting Colombo plan aid. It is not just a case of helping out a Canadian firm. It also helps the recipient country.

I do not want to leave it there. The minister will recall that when his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce was putting this legislation through the house he said that the purpose of it was-and the wording of the act will support this-to assist the Canadian producers to compete with the producers in other countries. It was in no sense a form of aid to recipient countries which might require assistance in developing their own economies. I think the matter should be clarified. There is a matter of government policy there because what the minister is now


claiming for section 21 of the export credits insurance legislation is something very different from what the house was led to believe when the legislation was put through and what I believe the legislation itself contains as its set purpose and objectives. I would hope that the minister would look further into the matter so that there will not be two views of the government that appear at least superficially to be in conflict on this point.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sure the minister to whom the hon. member for Ottawa West referred, if he were here, would agree with me that the act was intended to serve both purposes.

I was very interested in the discussion with respect to Canada joining the organization of American states. We in this group fully appreciate the caution with which the government is proceeding in this direction. There are political, financial and other implications that have to be seriously considered. It is not as simple a matter as it appears on the surface.
The minister said that this period of consideration would give the Canadian people an opportunity to discuss the question and express their views, and so on. Before the government makes a final decision in this connection will it give the house an opportunity to discuss the question and the members an opportunity to bring to the attention of the minister the opinions of the Canadian people they happen to represent in the various constituencies.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think if and when such a step were taken it would be debated in the house. There would be a resolution or motion; I am not just sure what form of procedure would be followed. I think the hon. member can take it for granted that there would be an opportunity for discussion.

S9. Colombo plan, $50,000,000.

I believe this is a vote for the Colombo plan. The only question I should like to ask on the appropriation is this. As the minister knows, when the Colombo plan was established, it was designed primarily for capital assistance and to make it easier for those countries which were being helped to help themselves. I have the impression, and there may have been circumstances which made this necessary, that over recent years the proportion of capital assistance has been declining in relation to the proportion of consumer assistance. Can the minister give

us the figures for the Colombo plan which would bear on that particular fact?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Any move in that direction has been because at least some of those countries, for example, India and Pakistan, which get between them $40 million of the $50 million, have pressed for commodities. They have done that for some years and they are pressing again this year. Mind you, the proceeds of the sale of those commodities are used on other projects, for example, hydroelectric projects, or various works of that kind.

Before this item carries will the minister advise the committee as to how much of the $50 million aid under the Colombo plan is made up of capital goods that go directly into the production for developing the economy of the recipient country. How much of it is made up of consumer goods? Of the part made up of consumer goods how much of that in turn is accompanied by an agreement for the provision of counterpart funds to be used in the development of the economy of the recipient country and how much of it has no strings attached at all?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: About half of the $50 million is expended directly on capital projects, about one quarter on wheat and the other quarter on such things as aluminum, copper and other commodities of that kind. The proceeds from the sales of wheat and metal and other commodities are used as counterpart funds for other projects in those countries.

90. West Indies assistance program, $1,500,000.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is the position of this program? I saw in the press this week, I believe, that the West Indies Federation had accepted delivery of one of the ships. I think it was the Royal Palm which was built at the Port Weller drydocks. Is there any other assistance over and above the additional ship that is being given and what is the position with respect to that ship now? When will it be completed and when will it be delivered?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The first ship, which has been named the Federal Maple, is now in operation in the West Indies. Over the week end I read in a West Indies magazine of the initial trip of this ship to the various islands. The other ship, which is called the Federal Palm, is now on the way to the West Indies. In addition, there will be technical assistance by way of provision of Canadian experts, $206,750, training of West Indians in Canada, $34,250, the development of deep water docking facilities at St. Vincent island, $950,000, the provision of port handling equipment at eight islands of the federation, $450,000, a
Supply-External Affairs survey of the natural resources of the island of Dominica, $50,000, and The University College of the West Indies, $700,000.

This vote shows a decrease of $3,760,000. We all know the reason for the decrease, but having in mind, for instance, the initiative that is taken in providing assistance to certain West Indies countries where the problem of economic underdevelopment characterizes the situation and bearing in mind, for instance, the kind of speech we had from the junior member or senior member from Halifax, has the government any plan to keep this form of assistance to the West Indies at the present level for next year, for instance? When we talk about assistance to these areas, unless there is some explanation a reduction of this sort possibly will be misconstrued in certain quarters. I would be interested to know whether the government has in mind further forms of assistance to other countries that do need it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The provision of $10 million was by way of a gift to the West Indies in order to help them when they got their independence. It was never designed as an annual payment or a payment every three years or for any set period. What will be done in the future has not yet been finally decided. Some time ago I referred to the possibility of a Colombo type program for the Caribbean area but I am not yet sure just what steps will be taken.

On this vote I would merely wish to express the hope that something more could be done. I think that we in Canada have a special interest in and perhaps even some responsibility for the West Indies as they achieve independent status. They are perhaps as close to us as any other member of the commonwealth, or will be geographically, when they join us. I think we can be expected to take a special interest in the development of this area. Presumably, as I have read, they will be joining the organization of American states and perhaps any assistance we could give to them would be within the context of hemisphere assistance.
I think it would be a very good thing if we could concentrate some of our aid in respect of this new member of the commonwealth, as we hope it will be. It will be no use for the minister to say that we did not do anything at all in our day because in those days the West Indies islands were colonies and they got their help from the colonial development fund. But now that they are becoming independent they have a special claim on us. I know that every country in

91. Special commonwealth Africa aid program, $3,500,000.

Mr. Chairman, with respect to vote 91 and possibly vote 92 I should first of all like to say how pleased I am to see this new item of $3,500,000 this year for special commonwealth Africa aid. I should like to ask the minister how this amount is broken down. As hon. members know, I had the honor of attending the commonwealth parliamentary conference in London earlier this year. The African delegates pointed out their desperate need for educational aid, for teachers, for courses of education in Canada and for agricultural training, all of which we in Canada can offer. Canada is a country with much that we can give to these new nations. Canada is a country greatly admired by them because of our achievements. It might be of interest to hon. members to know that in the country of Basutoland there is one university which was founded by the Roman Catholic church of Canada and is maintained by them. I think that Canadians should be very proud of the fact that in Basutoland there is a university founded and maintained by Canadians.
These African delegates pleaded with me to bring to the attention of the Canadian government their need for educational assistance and agricultural development. I would hope that the government through the minister would not only continue this amount but increase it with special emphasis on those things which they so much need.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: about $1.35 million over a two-year period. In addition, 17 technical advisers have been recruited, of whom 10 are already in Africa and eight more will be recruited shortly. Numerous additional requests are being investigated. We have 27 teachers in Africa altogether, 25 technical trainees in Canada and 53 students in Canada. I think the 53 include students coming here under this plan and also the commonwealth scholarship plan. We are currently discussing a number of specific requests for the building of schools, road programs and assistance in the medical field.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am glad that the hon. member for Wetaskiwin raised this question because I have a particular interest in another university in that area of the country. I refer to the one at Roma in Basutoland where Father Odilon Chevrier, a namesake and cousin of mine was for some years the rector of the university. I say the rest with some hesitation because I recall that when I was a boy my father set up a bursary or scholarship for the education of the first negro priest in the Catholic church. His name, I remember quite well, was Raphael Mohasi. He was ordained and has since passed away. Ever since that time coloured priests have been educated by virtue of that scholarship and have joined the ranks of the Oblates who are at the university in Roma. I felt that when the hon. member raised the question I might refer to this personal matter and I should at least pay tribute to the tremendous work done by the Oblates of Mary Immaculate at that university.
As the minister knows, they have a university here in Ottawa and their work in Basutoland specifically has been one not only of magnitude but has been a tremendous contribution to the inhabitants of that area. If there is any assistance that is going to the other university I am sure the minister, as well as the government, will want to give consideration to both of these universities.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, under this plan the assistance is arranged from government to government and not from the Canadian government to any individual institution. Now, if an application is made through the colonial office by these people in Basutoland we would be very glad to consider it. We have not felt we could start dealing with individuals or individual institutions in any one of these countries.

I think it should be noted just in this connection that not only is the government giving assistance, but the Oblate fathers themselves are doing work in Canada through Reverend Father Breault, who happens to come from my constituency

and who is the Vicar-General in a diocese in Basutoland. Canadian citizens are helping by their contributions towards the assistance of a very worthy project in this particular area. In addition, therefore, to the vote that we are providing tonight, it should be noted as the hon. member for Laurier recalls, that assistance is being provided by Canadian citizens. I can say that the Vicar-General, who happens to come from my constituency and who is engaged in collecting money to assist in the building of this area, is doing very excellent work. I strongly support the tribute that the hon. member for Laurier paid to the university, of which he is so distinguished a graduate and which my own son is attending.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wanted to ask here for a statement by the minister as to how much of this million dollars has been spent and how it has been divided as between the various universities.
