I should like to say a word about item 93 because I am a great believer in scholarships whether they are on a local level, whether they are exchange scholarships between various universities in Canada or exchange scholarships between universities in Canada and foreign universities or whether they are Canada council scholarships primarily in the cultural field or scholarships such as we are considering here under the commonwealth scholarship plan. I know, as one whose own education was assisted to a large degree by scholarships, of the economic assistance they provide. However, in this case I think we are more interested in the human relationships which stem from students visiting other universities being able to mix with the students, see how others live and think.
I should like to associate myself in extending congratulations to the government on this increase in the amount of money being expended for these scholarships in the coming year. This is certainly money well spent. There is only one matter I should like to raise. It arises out of a little story I heard when I was at the United Nations. Apparently some of the members of the commonwealth are being offered scholarships in the Soviet union, and there is the story of the Nigerian student who was the son of a prominent Nigerian family. This student went to study in the Soviet union. The reason I mention this story is that I sometimes wonder whether we utilize to the full our capacity to influence these students to our way of life, or the students who leave Canada to go abroad. I wonder whether we leave with them the impression that they have a moral obligation to be good ambassadors for Canada.
In this instance the young Nigerian student was practising boxing in the gym and unknown to him a picture was taken of him in a fighting position. This picture then appeared on a poster which proclaimed that this young negro from Nigeria had come to the Soviet union to learn about the great things going on there so he would be prepared to break the chains of slavery in the colonialized country from which he came. I think this is dishonest of course, and I use this illustration only to demonstrate the extent to which even in a case such as this the communist nations are utilizing their methods of propaganda.
My words are not directed primarily to the government but also to the universities themselves who make the selections, and to individuals who participate in this program. I think perhaps we have not utilized to the full our capacity to associate with these students coming to Canada from coast to coast and tried to demonstrate to them our

Supply-External Affairs way of life and our mode of thinking and, more important than that, why we live and think as we do.
Similarly, I think we should emphasize to all the people we send abroad that there is indeed room for them to be good ambassadors for Canada, as I am sure most of them are, because in their interrelationships at the university stage they are at a point in their lives when they are forming philosophies of life, and so forth, and these students coming to Canada and studying in our universities, then going back to their own native countries and assuming positions of leadership, will no doubt be very impressed with what they see and hear in Canada. I think this influence can be increased to a very great extent and I hope hon. members who have anything to do with the program will keep this point in mind.

99. Contribution to the United Nations relief and works agency for Palestine refugees in the near east, $500,000.

This is an item that has come before us now for some time year after year. It represents one of the great unsolved international social and economic problems of our time. Some one million refugees are covered in this particular area of activity. UNWRA or, as it is called, the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine, provides assistance for this number of people. Over the week end I noticed in the New York Times that Joe Johnson of the Carnegie foundation has been sent by the government of the United States to look into certain aspects of the problem. Perhaps I am wrong in saying that he has been sent by the government of the United States. Perhaps he was sent by the United Nations. In any event, that gentleman who has spent so much of his time on international problems has been sent to take a look at this particular question, the solution for which does not seem to exist at the present time. I wonder whether the minister is in a position to say what his expectancy is with regard to this matter. I know that it is an extremely difficult one. It certainly depends upon circumstances beyond the control of this nation. However, having seen these refugees in some of their camps in this area and knowing how they feel, knowing of their embittered state and how almost inhuman the situation is, altogether apart from what may be the provocations, I would say that we cannot go on endlessly with this problem existing. The longer a solution is delayed, the more difficult the problem is going to become. Canada has borne its share of the cost of maintaining UNWRA. However, I am sure the minister would expect an opposition at this time to inquire what progress is being made in providing a solution to this situation and what steps towards ultimate humanitarian liquidation are likely to eventuate.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid this problem is quite a long way from final solution. At each
90205-6-518
Supply-External Affairs session of the general assembly of the United Nations the whole situation is thoroughly canvassed and various remedies are proposed. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There are two matters that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister here. One of them concerns perhaps the most important commodity in the world, the commodity of water. As the minister appreciates, the United States and Canada are using more and more water for industrial and consumption purposes-more particularly industrial purposes-than ever before. I am concerned at the moment with the water levels in the port of Montreal. They have been discussed at some length by the authority but more particularly the situation is expressed in a report prepared by the Montreal port council in which some fear is expressed regarding the water level. This report is signed by the chairman, R. L. Dunsmore. There are two short references in this report to the water level which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. The first of these references reads as follows:
In the light of the low water levels last fall in the harbour, the criteria concerning water use priorities in the St. Lawrence river and lake Ontario established for the opening of the seaway were examined. It was noted that there were new rights of flood control, and water for hydroelectric power and navigational purposes up river from Montreal, and that the criterion concerning Montreal harbour water levels guaranteed only pre-seaway rights.
I doubt whether that is the juridical position, but whether it is or not makes no difference. The point is that there is fear in Montreal because of the lowering of the water level of the harbour.
It is further stated in this report as follows:
A ten thousand c.f.s. diversion means a drop of nearly half a foot in lake Ontario and at Montreal harbour.


The reason I bring this matter to the attention of the committee is that there is a clear obligation on the part of the government of Canada to see to it that water levels both upstream of the power development project in the international section as well as downstream in the St. Lawrence River is protected for navigation. That was clearly set out in the order of approval dated October 29, 1952 by the international joint commission.
Let me just place on Hansard the section which deals with that obligation and responsibility on the part of Canada, which reads as follows:
The works shall be so planned, located, constructed, maintained and operated as not to conflict with or restrain uses of the waters of the St. Lawrence river for purposes given preference over uses of water for power purposes by the treaty, namely, uses for domestic and sanitary purposes and uses for navigation, including the service of canals for the purposes of navigation, and shall be so planned, located, constructed, maintained and operated as to give effect to the provisions of this order.
In other words, notwithstanding the works on the international section, the first priority which must be granted and be given by the government of Canada is for the uses of domestic and sanitary purposes, and then next navigation, over and above power.
The international commission, having that in mind, established under this order a board of control to be known as the international St. Lawrence river board of control. The purposes and objects of that board were to make sure that the downstream interests as well as the upstream interests should in no way be affected.
Here I would like to pause to inform the minister that I believe the international joint commission has done a commendable job of work either through itself or through the board of control which I have mentioned.
On July 2, 1956, it issued a supplementary order of approval which deals with this matter, and which sets out what should be done in order to protect upstream and downstream interests. Perhaps I may just put the three recommendations of that order on the record. They are as follows:
(i)	A range of mean monthly elevations for lake Ontario of 244 feet (navigation season) to 248.0 feet as nearly as may be; and
(ii)	Criteria for a method of regulation of outflows and levels of lake Ontario applicable to the works in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river; and
(iii)	Plan of regulation No. 12-A-9, subject to minor adjustments that may result from further detailed study and evaluation by the commission;
The board of control working under the authority of that order has issued two volumes, one and two, dealing with the regulation of water levels of lake Ontario. The

reason I bring this subject to the attention of the minister is that at least the essential parts of this new plan 1958-A, have been put into operation. It is contained in this document and is a very detailed plan. I do not understand it and should like to say that it is an extremely difficult plan to understand.
However, I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the final recommendation contained in section VIII on page 43 of this volume, which is a part of the report to the international joint commission by the international St. Lawrence board of control. It reads as follows:
The board recommends adoption of the foregoing plan designated 1958-A, as the initial operating plan for regulation of the levels and outflows of lake Ontario having in mind that certain revisions may be necessary in the light of further studies and operating experience.
I am pleased that provision was included in this plan, namely, that certain revisions may be necessary in the light of further studies and operating experience. There is no doubt now that the plan, while on the whole it has worked satisfactorily, and while it is a difficult thing to control the level of outflows from lake Ontario, with all due respect to those who have prepared it is not working in the interests of navigation in the port of Montreal.
The port's council so found and the engineers who have studied the situation down there similarly think it is necessary to store a larger quantity of water in lake Ontario for the protection of downstream interests than is being stored at the present time.
I do not bring this situation to the attention of the minister in any critical way because, and I repeat, I think the international joint commission and the board of control have done a tremendous job in regard to a most difficult problem. I bring it to his attention because of its importance not only to the protection of upstream rights, but because of the necessary protection of downstream rights.
I understand that the power interests have a representative on the board of control. That is not the case in so far as navigation is concerned. I understand the reason for that is that since navigation is a matter which comes under the jurisdiction of the federal government it has been thought that the international joint commission and the Department of Transport would protect the rights of navigation. I have no doubt it is the intention of the Department of Transport to ensure that the interests of navigation are protected, but I bring this situation to the attention of the minister because of the report of the Montreal council. I should like to ask the minister
90205-6-518J
Supply-External Affairs to bring this fact to the attention of the international joint commission so there will be no lowering of the water level at the port of Montreal, because the slightest lowering of this level as a result of works and upstream ports, may be costly from an economical standpoint to the development of the port of Montreal.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Since I come from one of Canada's leading ports myself I have been greatly concerned about this problem, particularly last year. I do not know that it has been so pressing in the summer of 1961. But the procedures and principles for determining release in the future are under consideration by the international joint commission at the present time. The international St. Lawrence river board of control is taking a review of plan of regulation 1958-A, to which the hon. member for Laurier has referred. General McNaughton announced that this review is being made when he appeared before the standing committee on external affairs on June 14 of this year. It is expected that in due course the commission, in the light of the board's review, will report to governments on what alterations, if any, should be made in the plan of regulation. We have this situation very much in mind. I am hoping that it can be solved to the satisfaction of the city of Montreal.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The other matter that I wanted to discuss, and I will do it as briefly as I can, is one that also comes under the international joint commission. It is one that has been discussed in the house from time to time. I will not deal with the subject save and except in so far as it refers to the international joint commission. I refer to the important development of the Champlain-Richelieu cut-off. I mention it from an entirely different angle because, as the minister has seen in the press recently, there is a general feeling in the United States that they should use their internal canals to a far greater extent than they have in the past. It has been stated on more than one occasion that it is the intention of the United States to do one of two things. First, to develop the Richelieu river from lake Champlain into the St. Lawrence river at Sorel or second, into the port of Montreal by way of an overland route, and from thence to use the St. Lawrence seaway that has been developed so that navigation can be continued to Chicago and down the Illinois and the Mississippi to the ports along the Gulf of Mexico. Therefore, there would be a use of the United States ports on their internal canals, either by the route which I have mentioned or the other alternative which is under serious

Supply-External Affairs consideration in the United States, namely the deepening of the New York state barge canal.
They have gone so far as to say that whether Canada determines this or not they intend to go ahead and develop that route. If, as it has been stated in congress and elsewhere, they develop the New York state barge canal rather than use the St. Lawrence seaway by way of the Champlain-Richelieu cut-off, then I believe that serious consideration should be given by the government to the harm that might befall the economy if the whole eastern part of the seaway were by-passed by traffic in that manner.
The deepening of the New York barge canal would cost infinitely more money than the development of the Champlain-Richelieu cutoff. Recently a statement apeared in La Presse of July 15, 1961, which I have here, in which the inertia of the federal government is attacked for the lack of consideration of the Champlain cut-off.
I said at the beginning that I did not intend to get into a contentious debate and I do not think it should be done at this stage. What I bring to the attention of the minister is this. It seems to me this whole matter can be avoided if the government will only set up a board of engineers to consider making surveys of a waterway from the international boundary downstream to the St. Lawrence river. If that is done-and I understand it can be done at very little cost-then at least we shall be co-operating with the United States interests.
I have also learned that the United States corps of engineers have started surveys on their side of the line and have obtained a great deal of information in so far as Canadian conditions are concerned with reference to locks, bridges, and the depth of water. Therefore, I only repeat here what has been said from this side of the house, namely that the government give additional consideration to the establishment at very little cost of a survey to ascertain where the most economical route would be because five of them have been found as alternative routes by the international joint commission in its interim report of 1937, and, next, the economics of this project.
The international joint commission dealt with it at some length in the interim report. There are two volumes which I have in my possession. In this interim report they asked that they be given jurisdiction in this matter when the St. Lawrence seaway had been completed. As the minister knows, the seaway has been in operation since 1959. It seems to those who have studied the question that


the time has arrived to ask the commission to continue its work which was interrupted in 1937.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This question is under study by the several departments of government which are concerned but as yet we have had no report on that study. I am very keenly aware of the interest being taken in the whole project.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I just add this. I know a study is being made by the several departments of government, but I have kept away from that. I am bringing to the attention of the minister the fact that the body to deal with this matter will be the international joint commission. I am not saying that it is, because I would not want to do the slightest thing that would dissuade the government from going ahead with this study. But since the international joint commission had it under consideration previously it may well be that it is the proper and logical body to deal with this matter at this time. If the government should come to that conclusion even before the report has been received from the interdepartmental committee I am sure it would be doing a great service to the Canadian people, in the light of what is happening in the United States at the present time.

516. Assessment for the United Nations Congo ad hoc account for 1961 in an amount of $3,080,733 U.S., notwithstanding that payment may exceed or fall short of the equivalent in Canadian dollars, estimated as of May, 1961, which is, $3,044,150.
This is a very large amount. Would the minister care to make any comment having regard to the troubles that apparently still exist in the Congo?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a good example of the high cost of getting results in the Congo. The United Nations operation in the Congo, which is known as ONUC, was established by the security council in July, 1960. The secretary general was called upon

to furnish wide-scale assistance, both military and civilian, to the Belgian Congo, which became independent on June 30 of last year.
To meet the initial costs of the Congo operation he relied heavily on his authority to borrow from the working capital fund and the reserves of the special fund and the expanded program of technical assistance. At the first part of the fifteenth session of the general assembly last fall the secretary general presented estimates for the Congo operation for the last six months of 1960 in the amount of over $66 mililon. The United Kingdom, the United States and Canada agreed to waive reimbursement for certain claims in order to reduce total costs of the operation to be assessed. In accordance with a decision by the cabinet, Canada waived some $600,000 representing initial airlift costs. We took and are still taking a very active part in the airlift to the Congo. As a result of these special contributions, the general assembly approved a budget of $48.5 million for assessment on members. It took no decision on the 1961 Congo costs until the resumed session of the general assembly in March and April of this year. The secretary general's estimates for 1961, which were submitted just prior to that resumed session, totalled $135 million. The advisory committee recommended that this amount be reduced to $120 million for 1961.
At the close of the resumed session, the general assembly adopted a resolution authorizing the expenditure of $100 million U.S. for the first ten months in 1961 and the general assembly will be required to consider the costs for the remaining two months of 1961 at its session which begins on September 19.
Canada believes that a decision of the security council which entails financial commitments imposes a mandatory obligation on members to pay. In the discussions on the financing of ONUC, Canada pressed these views but was forced to agree to compromises by which ad hoc accounts for ONUC were set up for 1960 and 1961. The resolution setting up the 1960 ad hoc account contained a paragraph which noted that the expenses were an obligation on all members in accordance with article 17 (2) of the charter. The resolution creating the 1961 ad hoc account, however, was watered down and while acknowledging the Congo costs as expenses of the organization it omitted reference to the legally binding nature of the obligation to pay.
The Congo expenses are assessed according to the regular scale of assessment of the organization. As a result of voluntary contributions by the United States, however, certain members with low assessment rates and in receipt of technical assistance were made eligible for rebates. The amount of these re-
Supply-External Affairs bates in 1960 was 50 per cent but the formula was revised for 1961 to give up to 80 per cent rebates.
The Canadian government has indicated Canada's strong support for the United Nations operation in the Congo from its inception. All the political considerations point to the necessity for continued Canadian support for United Nations action in the Congo. Early payment of the Canadian assessment for the 1961 costs is particularly important in order to give the organization much needed funds to keep the operation going in the face of a threatened heavy deficit resulting from the failure of certain members, particularly the Soviet bloc, to pay their assessments. For this reason the Canadian assessment for the 1961 Congo costs is included in the first supplementary estimates for 1961-62.
On the basis of the regular scale of assessment Canada's share of the $100 million costs of the operation in 1961 up to the end of October, that is, for the first ten months, is $3,080,733 U.S. This estimate provides for a contribution in that amount converted at the current rate of exchange.

I thank the minister for his explanation although if he looks at the language and having regard to the amount of money involved I think he will recognize that the language is somewhat loose when it refers to an estimate as of May, 1961. Even one month's expenditures are consequential so it would be important to know whether the cutoff date is May 1 or the end of May 1961.
